docs.title: Tunarr
docs.text:
Create live TV channels from media on your Plex/Jellyfin servers, and more!

Configure your channels, programs, commercials, and settings using the Tunarr web UI.

Watch your channels by adding the spoofed Tunarr HDHomeRun tuner to Plex, Jellyfin, or Emby. Or utilize generated M3U files with any 3rd party IPTV player app.

  • Installation

    Get Tunarr up and running with Docker or standalone binaries.

  • Setup

    Initial configuration and connecting your first media source.

  • Channels

    Create and configure your virtual TV channels.

  • Scheduling

    Organize your channel programming with powerful scheduling tools.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text:
Tunarr was originally a fork of dizqueTV (which in itself was a fork of other projects!) which evolved into a near-complete rewrite. This project was born out of both a love for TV and an appreciation for the work put into dizqueTV and its predecessors.

Tunarr has the following goals:

  • Modernize the stack, both backend and frontend
  • Stabilize the program, fix bugs, and improve performance
  • Modernize and "prettify" the Web UI
  • And of course, add a ton of great new features!

docs.title: Transcoding
docs.text: Tunarr uses FFmpeg to transcode or remux content when generating channel streams. Transcoding settings are split across two levels: channel-level settings that control the streaming architecture, and transcode configuration settings that control codec, resolution, bitrate, and hardware acceleration.

docs.title: Channel Stream Mode
docs.text:
The stream mode determines the overall pipeline architecture Tunarr uses to produce a channel's output. Available modes include HLS (recommended), HLS alt, HLS Direct, and MPEG-TS. Each mode has different characteristics in terms of reliability, CPU usage, and client compatibility.

See Channel Transcoding Settings for a full explanation of each mode and guidance on choosing one.

docs.title: Transcode Configurations
docs.text:
A transcode configuration is a reusable set of encoding parameters (codec, resolution, bitrate, hardware acceleration, audio settings, etc.) that can be assigned to one or more channels. This is where you configure how Tunarr encodes the output stream.

See Transcode Configs for a detailed breakdown of every setting, including hardware acceleration options for NVIDIA, Intel, AMD, and macOS.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Channels are the core of Tunarr. Each channel acts like a virtual TV station with its own programming schedule, stream settings, and EPG data.

Click the NEW button to create your first channel, which will take you to the Channel Properties page.

Save creates the channel and opens its programming page; the fields are locked until it exists. When you edit a channel, Save is enabled once something has changed, and "Reset changes" puts the saved values back. Switching between the editor's tabs keeps your changes, and leaving the page with unsaved changes asks first.

The edit tabs are Properties, Flex, Guide, Streaming, and Watermark. Each has its own address, so you can bookmark or share a tab and use the browser's Back and Forward buttons between tabs. These tab changes keep the same unsaved form; Save applies changes from all tabs together. Older ?tab=epg and ?tab=ffmpeg links open Guide and Streaming respectively.

  • Properties

    Configure basic channel settings like name, number, icon, and group.

  • Programming

    Add shows, movies, and other content to your channel's schedule.

  • Flex

    Configure filler content to play during gaps in your schedule.

  • Guide

    Customize how your channel appears in electronic program guides.

  • Transcoding

    Configure stream modes and transcoding settings per channel.

  • Watermarks

    Add logo overlays and watermarks to your channel's video output.

docs.title: Working with several channels
docs.text:
On the Channels page (on a computer; phones show the channel cards without checkboxes), tick the box on each channel you want, or the box in the header to select the whole page. The table then shows how many are selected and:

  • Delete asks once, listing the channels, and deletes them all. If some fail, the message names each one that was not deleted and why.
  • Hide from guide and Show in guide turn the channel's Stealth mode on or off for every selected channel. Stealth mode hides a channel from the guide, the HDHomeRun tuner and the M3U playlist; you can still stream it directly or redirect to it. Only the channels that need the change are saved, and each keeps its other settings, including its filler lists.

The selection clears when the action finishes and when you change page.

docs.title: Updating channel relations through the API
docs.text: PUT /api/channels/{id} keeps saved filler attachments and subtitle preferences when fillerCollections or subtitlePreferences is omitted. Send an explicit [] to clear that relation, or a nonempty array to replace it. The remaining required channel fields are unchanged. The channel editor sends a relation only when you edit it, including an empty list when you remove the last subtitle preference.

docs.text:
1. Create a new channel with Properties

  3. Use Scheduling Tools to organize your lineup

docs.title: Guide
docs.text: Tunarr generates an XMLTV-formatted Electronic Program Guide (EPG) for all active channels. This guide data can be consumed by media clients (Plex, Jellyfin, Emby, Channels DVR, etc.) to display program schedules and metadata alongside the live stream.

docs.title: XMLTV Output
docs.text:
Tunarr writes XMLTV data to an .xml file in the data directory, but clients should always consume it via the API endpoint rather than reading the file directly:

http://<tunarr-host>:<port>/api/xmltv.xml

The full URL is also shown in the Tunarr web UI under Settings > Guide, below the XMLTV output path. Point your client's guide data source at this URL to populate the program guide.

docs.title: When the guide is updated
docs.text:
• The whole guide is rebuilt on the schedule in Settings > Guide and when you refresh it there. The schedule is the Refresh interval counted from Refreshes start at (server time), around the clock: a 4 hour interval from 03:00 rebuilds at 03:00, 07:00, 11:00, 15:00, 19:00 and 23:00; a 6 hour interval from 23:00 at 05:00, 11:00, 17:00 and 23:00; a 24 hour interval from 03:00 once a day at 03:00. The defaults, every 4 hours from 00:00, rebuild at midnight and every 4 hours after. An interval that doesn't divide 24 starts again at that hour each day, so the gap before it is shorter: a 5 hour interval from 04:00 rebuilds at 00:00, 04:00, 09:00, 14:00 and 19:00. A full rebuild reads every program in the guide window, so on a busy server pick an hour when nobody watches. Saving these settings moves the schedule at once and rebuilds the guide straight away.
  • Each rebuild writes Guide length (hours) worth of guide, and nothing adds to it until the next rebuild, so Guide length has to be at least two hours longer than the time between rebuilds: this conservatively covers clock rollbacks of up to two hours, including Antarctica/Troll. The settings page flags a shorter guide and the API refuses it. An interval of 24 hours or more rebuilds once a day, so a 26-hour guide covers it. Settings saved before this check are rebuilt often enough for their guide (a 24 hour interval with a 12-hour guide every 10 hours), and the server logs a warning at startup. Legacy guide lengths below three hours are treated as three hours at runtime without rewriting the saved value.
  • Upgrading from a version where the rebuilds stopped at midnight: a start hour other than 00:00 with an interval under 24 hours now rebuilds around the clock, so it can rebuild more often than before (every 6 hours from 18:00 was once a day, at 18:00, and now is 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00). For one rebuild a day, set the interval to 24.
  • Daylight saving time: the hours are the server's clock hours. When the clocks go forward, a rebuild set for an hour that is skipped (02:00 in the US) runs at the hour after it, once. When they go back, an hour that happens twice runs once.
  • Saving a channel updates that channel's entries straight away. The other channels keep the entries they already had, so a change to a program's details since then, from a library scan for example, appears at the next scheduled rebuild. Rebuilding every channel on each save made Live TV pause while channels were saved.
  • Changing a setting under Settings > Guide updates every channel at the next write.

The authenticated POST /api/xmltv/flush endpoint waits up to 30 seconds for queued Plex guide notifications to finish. It returns 200 when done or 202 while work remains.

docs.title: Program Metadata
docs.text:
Tunarr populates the XMLTV output with program metadata sourced from your media libraries, including:

  • Program title and episode title
  • Description / plot summary
  • Air date and year
  • Content rating
  • Cast and crew credits
  • Genres — included under the XMLTV <category> tag, sourced from the genre metadata attached to each program in your media library. Clients that display genre information in their guide (e.g., Channels DVR) will pick these up automatically.

Info

Genre data is only available for programs that have genre metadata in the originating media source. If a program's entry in your media server has no genres attached, the <category> tag will not be present for that program in the XMLTV output.

docs.title: Flex
docs.text:
Flex is an optional block of time that is used to separate two episodes of television. One reason to use Flex time is to create commercial breaks after each episode to simulate traditional television.

There are a few ways to create Flex time such as Time Slots. When you have Flex time but no Filler Content configured, the Channel Fallback shown in the screenshot below will be used. You can optionally select the upload button to choose your own custom fallback image.

Please see the Filler Lists page for details on creating your first list.

Once you have a Filler list created, you can select the list you'd like to use on a particular channel.

Once you have a Filler list added to a channel, it will only be used when there is Flex time scheduled, such as when using Time Slots with the Pad Times feature. Tuning in during a gap starts as quickly as tuning in during a program: the start of the gap is prepared ahead, the same way a program's is, and a fallback image uploaded in the web UI is read straight from the server's disk. With NVIDIA, Intel QSV or VAAPI hardware acceleration the fallback image still starts at normal speed, because those pipelines can't prepare a still image ahead.

docs.title: Gap music
docs.text:
The channel fallback can play music under its image. Build a filler list of tracks from a music library (add whole artists or albums, or single tracks), then choose it as Gap music next to the fallback image.

  • During flex time that no filler fills, the image shows while the list's tracks play one after another. Each gap plays tracks this channel hasn't played recently first.
  • Every track is normalized to the same loudness (about -24 LUFS, typical for TV), so loud and quiet recordings sit at an even level. Programs themselves are not normalized.
  • A track fades in, and fades out when the gap ends before the track does.
  • Don't also add the list as filler on the same channel: filler tracks play as programs with their album art instead.

The music library has to be enabled and scanned under Sources first.

docs.title: Artist and title
docs.text:
With Show the artist and title checked (the default), the track that's playing is shown as "♪ Artist — Title" in a dark strip along the bottom of the fallback image.

  • The strip is in the same place on every channel, centred near the bottom edge, so keep important detail out of the bottom tenth of your fallback image. It's sized from the image's height, so it scales with it.
  • Long names are cut short with "...".
  • The text uses a font bundled with Tunarr (M+ Rounded 1c) that covers Latin, Greek, Cyrillic and Japanese. A name with characters it doesn't have, such as Korean, shows no text rather than empty boxes.
  • It needs an ffmpeg build with the drawtext filter. Without one, gaps show the image without the text.

docs.title: Gaps in the guide
docs.text: In the XMLTV guide, a gap shows a picture: the Guide Picture for Gaps if you set one, otherwise the fallback image, otherwise the channel logo. Apps such as Plex keep one picture per guide entry and crop it to both tall and wide tiles. A wide fallback image with text across it loses its edges in tall tiles, so for the guide picture use a square image with its content in the middle third of the width and the middle half of the height.

docs.title: Programming
docs.text:
After creating a new channel, you will be presented with a blank Programming page.

Select "ADD MEDIA".

Select the library you'd like to pull media from.

Add all of the shows you'd like this channel to include.

If you'd like to add all episodes from a show, select "ADD SERIES".

If you'd only like to include specific seasons, expand the show by selecting the carrot on the left and select "ADD ALL" on each season you'd like to include.

If you'd like to add specific episodes but not the entire season, expand the season by selecting the carrot on the left and select "ADD EPISODE".

Expand the menu on the right to view a summary of your changes.

Select "ADD ITEMS" to save your changes.

By default, your shows are ordered alphabetically (by show name) and episodes within are in proper season order. In this example, we have two shows and the first show will play in its entirety progressing from specials through all seasons, and only then will the next show start playing.

To make the viewing experience more interesting and authentic, you will want to use Tunarr's scheduling tools to reorder and group content.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Choose a channel a name. Optionally, you can also add a thumbnail by uploading an image or providing an image URL. This will be the logo visible within your IPTV client's channel guide. Transparent .png files are supported.

docs.title: Channel Icon
docs.text:
The channel icon has three states:

  • Custom icon -- Upload an image or provide a URL. This image appears in your IPTV client's channel guide, watermark overlays, and the Tunarr UI.
  • Default logo -- When no custom icon is set, Tunarr shows its default logo as a fallback. This is the default behavior.
  • No icon -- Click the X button next to the icon preview to remove the icon entirely. In this state, no icon is included in the M3U playlist, XMLTV guide data, or watermark overlay. To restore the default logo after removing the icon, click the restore button.

An uploaded icon's address ends in a version taken from the image (…_icon.png?v=…). Uploading a different image gives it a new address, so clients that cache images by address, such as Plex and its apps, load the new one instead of keeping the old. Icons uploaded before this was added keep their old address until they are uploaded again.

On-Demand will allow your channels to behave similar to streaming services, where the watch states will only progress while you're actively viewing the channel. This is disabled by default, which means by default channels will behave similar to traditional televison where watch states will progress without you actively viewing the channel.

Click the "Flex" tab if you'd like to configure optional filler content to play in-between episodes.

docs.title: Channel Transcoding Settings
docs.text: Open the channel editor's Streaming tab for stream mode, transcode config, audio, and subtitles. Logo overlays are configured in the separate Watermark tab.

docs.title: Stream Mode
docs.text:
Tunarr supports several different stream modes that can be set at the channel level.

Info

No matter which stream mode you choose for a channel, clients which require an MPEG-TS stream will still work.

docs.title: HLS (recommended)
docs.text: HLS is the default streaming mode for a channel. In our testing, it is generally the most reliable and efficient. It is akin to ErsatzTV's "HLS Segmenter" mode.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: This mode creates a single FFMPEG process, per-program. The process applies all transcoding configuration necessary. Tunarr manages interleaving these processes to create seamless m3u8 playlists for playback.

docs.title: Things to consider
docs.text: In our testing, we've found this mode to be both efficient and reliable. That said, it is also the newest mode introduced to Tunarr, so there might be some kinks to work out.

docs.title: HLS alt
docs.text: HLS alt (name pending!) is another HLS streaming mode, which operates a little differently. This mode is akin to ErsatzTV's "HLS Segmenter V2" mode.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: This mode creates two FFMPEG processes. The first runs per-program and applies scaling/cropping, watermarks, frame rate changes, etc, but outputs a rawvideo stream. The second process concatenates all of these together while also applying bit rate limits and codec changes.

docs.title: Things to consider
docs.text: The downside to this mode is that the one of the steps (the per-program process) requires software encoding. This can put a lot of stress on certain systems. The stream setup can also lead to quality loss, due to generation loss. However, it does have the potential to create a more reliable / robust stream.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: This mode does not perform any stream normalization. When the channel m3u8 playlist is requested, it returns a playlist with a single item URL set to the duration of the current item in the channel. The URL returns a direct stream of the item, remuxed to the container set as HLS Direct output format under Settings > Playback (MPEG-TS, MKV, or MP4).

docs.title: Things to consider
docs.text: Because this mode does not perform stream normalization, there may be issues when transitioning between programs; the mode requires clients to essentially "reset" themselves between each program for transitions to function as expected. Some clients that are known to work in this mode are Jellyfin and MPV, but there are almost certainly others.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: HLS Direct v2 works like standard HLS mode, but without transcoding. Rather than returning a single-item m3u8 pointing directly to the program stream (as HLS Direct does), it produces a proper continuous HLS playlist of segmented chunks — the same structure as the regular HLS mode. No codec conversion or normalization is applied; the source content is remuxed directly into the segments.

docs.title: Things to consider
docs.text:
Users who want direct streaming without transcoding may find this mode more compatible than HLS Direct, particularly with clients that do not rely on FFmpeg's HLS demuxer implementation. Because the output is a standard segmented HLS playlist, clients that expect that structure should handle program transitions more gracefully than they would with HLS Direct.

As with HLS Direct, no stream normalization is applied, so mixed source formats (different codecs, resolutions, frame rates) across lineup items may cause playback issues depending on the client.

docs.title: MPEG-TS
docs.text: This mode is the closest to the DizqueTV experience.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text: It consists of two FFMPEG processes, one which performs the per-program transcode, outputting an mpeg-ts stream and one which concatenates this raw stream together and outputs it.

docs.title: Things to consider
docs.text: If this mode was "good enough" we probably wouldn't have spent time implementing the other modes! There are a lot of potential issues with this mode; too many to list here.

docs.title: Audio tracks (switchable audio in Plex Live TV)
docs.text:
Audio tracks (under Audio & Subtitles on the channel's Streaming tab) gives a channel a fixed set of audio tracks: up to four language codes (ISO 639-2, such as eng, jpn), in order. Every program, gap (the offline picture, with or without gap music), error screen and commercial on the channel then carries exactly these tracks, in this order, each tagged with its language.

Plex Live TV keeps the audio tracks it sees when you tune in for the whole session, and ends the session if the stream restarts. So a channel only gets a working audio menu when the tracks never change. With the setting:

  • Plex picks each viewer's preferred audio language. It uses the account's preferred audio language from the list. Viewers can still switch tracks in the player's audio menu.
  • A program with that language uses its own track for the slot. Among several tracks in that language, commentary tracks are skipped; then the selected, the default, or the first track wins.
  • A program without that language repeats its main audio in that slot, so the menu still has the same entries. The repeated track is processed once (volume, loudness normalization) and copied into each slot that uses it.
  • Every track is encoded with the channel's transcode configuration (codec, bitrate, channels, sample rate). Each extra track costs one more audio encode.
  • Every track is in the .ts stream Plex reads from the start. That stream waits up to 15 seconds for a track whose first audio comes a little late, instead of failing to start.

Leave the field empty for one audio track, the program's own, as before.

An anime channel

eng, jpn gives every program an English and a Japanese track. English comes first, so it's the default for players that don't pick a language. Dual-audio episodes offer both; English-only and Japanese-only episodes repeat their one language in the other slot.

Info

HLS Direct v2 copies each program's own tracks unchanged, so it can't offer a fixed set; the field is disabled for that mode. HLS, HLS alt and MPEG-TS support it.

docs.title: Subtitle preferences
docs.text:
Enable subtitles under Audio & Subtitles, then choose whether the channel uses global or custom preferences. The global preview shows the saved list from Settings > Captions & audio. Global changes apply when future streams select subtitles; they do not interrupt a program already playing.

Custom preferences use only this channel's list. Switching to global retains the custom rows, including unsaved edits, so switching back restores them. Save persists the selected mode and any edited custom rows. An intentionally empty custom list keeps the stream mode's existing fallback and does not use the global list. Turn Enable subtitles off to disable subtitles for the channel.

A nonempty inherited list tries each row's language, filter and external/image flags independently. None rows are skipped; no matching row means no subtitle. HLS Direct v2 only supports text output. Existing explicit stream-selection profiles keep precedence in profile-based playback; global preferences do not enable profile support in Direct v2 or change extraction/caption/WebVTT gates.

The fixed Audio tracks layout above stays per channel and has no global default.

docs.title: Captions for this channel
docs.text:
Captions for this channel (under Audio & Subtitles on the channel's Streaming tab) tries closed-caption options on one channel, a test channel for example, without changing them for every channel. Closed captions for HDHomeRun clients must be turned on under Settings > Captions & audio; that switch stays the one for every channel. Changes take effect from the channel's next program.

  • Test pattern on this channel: replaces this channel's captions with the numbered test pattern. Other channels keep their captions. When the test pattern under Settings > Captions & audio is on, every channel shows it, whatever this switch says.
  • Use own caption look: gives the channel its own caption alignment and caption appearance. The fields show the global look; a setting you change becomes this channel's own, and only this channel's captions change. Turned off, the channel follows the global look again.
  • Copy to all channels: makes this channel's look the global one, for every channel without a look of its own. Use it once a look works in your player.
  • Reset to global: drops the channel's own look and keeps its test pattern switch.

A setting the channel doesn't change follows the global one, so a later change on the Settings > Captions & audio page still reaches it.

docs.title: Channel Watermarks
docs.text:
Channels can have watermarks to aid in recreating a classic TV experience.

Open the channel editor's Watermark tab to enable and configure its overlay. These controls are separate from Streaming; the HLS Direct stream modes still disable watermarks.

There are many ways to customize watermarks for a channel. Here are some details on specific options:

docs.title: Watermark Period
docs.text: This value can be used to fade a channel's watermark in/out every N minutes.

docs.title: Watermark on leading edge
docs.text: When using intermittent watermarks, use this option to control whether the watermark begins in a visible (true) or hidden (false) state.

docs.title: Total watermark duration
docs.text:
This option controls the absolute duration the watermark can be displayed for a given program segment of a channel. Its value takes precedence over the 'watermark period' but does not disable it. For instance, you could configure a watermark period of 5 minutes with total duration of 45 mins. On a show that is one hour, the watermark will fade in/out for the first 45 minutes and then be hidden for the final 15 minutes.

For output resolution, bitrate, and buffer size, choose a transcode configuration on the channel's Streaming tab.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
Once you have your channels created in Tunarr, you're ready to watch them! Tunarr works with a variety of clients through its HDHomeRun emulation and M3U playlist support.

  • Plex

    Add Tunarr as an HDHomeRun tuner in Plex to watch channels with full DVR integration.

  • Jellyfin

    Configure Jellyfin to use Tunarr channels via HDHomeRun or M3U.

docs.title: Other Clients
docs.text:
Tunarr generates M3U playlists that work with any IPTV player. Some recommended apps:

Platform App iOS / Apple TV UHF Android TV TiviMate Cross-platform VLC

docs.title: Connection Methods
docs.text: Tunarr supports two ways to connect clients:

docs.title: HDHomeRun Emulation
docs.text:
Tunarr emulates an HDHomeRun network tuner, allowing media servers like Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby to discover it automatically. This provides the most seamless integration with full guide data.

Under Settings > Tuner, Network discovery turns the automatic discovery on or off (it needs a restart), and Tuner count sets how many tuners Tunarr reports. Plex plays at most that many channels at once.

docs.title: M3U Playlists
docs.text:
For IPTV apps and other players, Tunarr generates M3U playlist files. Access them at:

  • All channels: http://your-tunarr-ip:8000/api/channels/m3u
  • XMLTV guide: http://your-tunarr-ip:8000/api/xmltv

docs.title: Jellyfin
docs.text:
Once you have your channels created with programming/shows added, head over to Jellyfin. The following pictures show step-by-step how connect Tunarr to your Jellyfin server.

1. Locate "Hamburger" menu on the Jellyfin homepage 2. Locate the "Dashboard" menu item under "Administration" 3. Locate the "Live TV" menu item under "Live TV" in the sidebar

At this point, Jellyfin will ask for your tuner type - we recdommend selecting HD Homerun.

Note

Tunarr supports M3U and HDHR style connections from clients. However, some users have experienced stability issues at program boundaries when using Tunarr as an M3U tuner in Jellyfin. This seems to occur when Jellyfin is not transcoding / remuxing the incoming stream and seems related to the following issues: jellyfin/jellyfin-ffmpeg#57 and trac.ffmpeg.org/ticket/5419

You can then select "Detect My Devices," and Jellyfin may be able to detect your Tunarr instance and its IP address. If it does not, you can fill in your info manually. Use the following format replacing serverIP with your server's IP address and chosen port (if using Docker): e.g. http://serverIP:8000

Once you have entered your server's URL and port, you will have to add the XMLTV Guide.

  1. First select Add Provider.
  2. Choose XMLTV.
  3. A screen asking for several items and categories will appear - you generally don't have to change these unless you know what you're doing. What we care about is the first "File or URL" textbox.
  4. In this textbox, use the following template replacing serverIP with your Tunarr servers IP address: e.g. http://serverIP:8000/api/xmltv.xml.

If you only have one instance of Tunarr running, you can leave the "Enable for all tuner devices" checked.

If you have more than one instance, you can uncheck this and then apply this guide to only the tuners you select.

⚠ You can overwrite tuners' channels if you apply more than one guide with the same channel mappings to all tuners. ⚠

Be careful when assigning if this applies to you!

Select "Save" and Jellyfin should then return you to the Live TV screen and show you it is updating the guide info.

To see if your channels and settings were applied, go back to your main Jellyfin page by selecting the Home icon in the upper left with your server's name.

You should now see a "Live TV" card in your My media section - select it!

From here, you should see all shows that are playing on your channels under the Programs tab, or you can choose to see individual channels or guides from the other tabs.

Play your channel by hovering over the channel icon and selecting the play icon.

Happy watching! 📺

docs.title: Plex
docs.text:
Once you have your channels created with programming/shows added, head over to Plex > Settings icon > Manage > Live TV & DVR > Set Up Plex Tuner.

Plex should already detect Tunarr and you should see your servers IP address. If you do not, select "Don't see your HDHomeRun device? Enter its network address manually". Use the following format replacing serverIP with your servers IP address: e.g. http://serverIP:8000

Once your server is shown, select "Have an XMLTV guide on your server? Click here to use it."

In the "XMLTV GUIDE" field, use the following template replacing serverIP with your Tunarr servers IP address: e.g. http://serverIP:8000/api/xmltv.xml

Select "Continue"

Your channels should automatically be mapped. Select "Continue".

Plex should now display your Tunarr channels in the Live TV section. Select "View Guide" to be brought directly there.

docs.title: Guide updates
docs.text:
When a Plex media source has Send guide updates on, Tunarr asks that Plex server to reload its guide after each guide write. Writes less than 10 seconds apart, such as saving several channels in a row, lead to one ask, 10 seconds after the last. An ask made while Tunarr starts waits until Plex can download the guide. Every Plex server is asked at the same time, so one that fails or doesn't answer doesn't hold up the others. A failed ask is tried three times, 5 and then 15 seconds apart. If all three fail, Plex keeps its guide until the next guide write. If Plex refuses Tunarr's token (HTTP 401 or 403), or the media source has no token, Tunarr doesn't try again and logs a warning to check that media source's Plex token. The next guide write asks again.

A script that saves channels and then checks Plex's guide can call POST /api/xmltv/flush once its saves have returned. It answers when the guide writes those saves started have finished and Plex has been asked, or after 30 seconds at the latest. The status is 200 when everything finished and 202 when it stopped waiting with something still under way. The answer has done (false if it stopped waiting) and, for each Plex server asked, how the ask ended: reloaded, no_live_tv, auth_failed, failed, or pending if it hadn't finished. For example: {"done": true, "servers": [{"name": "Plex", "outcome": "reloaded"}]}.

docs.title: Posters in the guide
docs.text:
Plex's apps load guide pictures (programme posters, channel logos) themselves, from the addresses in the XMLTV file. Those addresses start with the one Plex used to fetch the guide. If that address only works on the server, such as http://127.0.0.1:8000, the apps can't load the pictures and show plain titles instead.

Gaps between programmes (flex) show the channel's offline picture, which is what airs during them, or the channel's logo when it has none.

A new channel logo appears in Plex after Plex next refreshes the guide: daily by default, right away with Refresh Guide in Plex's Live TV & DVR settings, or when Tunarr asks it to after a guide change (the media source's Send guide updates). A guide refresh keeps playing Live TV streams; only changing the channel map ends them.

To fix this, set Public address for guide pictures (Settings → Guide) to an address the apps can reach, such as https://tunarr.example.com. The guide's picture links then use it. Plex keeps fetching the guide from its usual address. The picture paths (/media/artwork/…, /api/programs/<id>/artwork/<type>, /api/credits/<id>/artwork/<type> and /images/…) must be reachable at that address without a login.

Images uploaded in the web UI (channel logos, offline pictures) are saved with that address too, so they load in Plex's apps even when you upload them from a browser on the server (localhost) or behind a proxy that terminates HTTPS. Without it, an upload gets the address the browser used, and behind such a proxy Tunarr sees plain http://. Images uploaded before you set it keep their saved address; upload them again to change it.

Each time Tunarr writes the guide, it saves every programme's poster as a file in the media/artwork folder of its data directory and links the guide to it, such as /media/artwork/<id>-poster.jpg?v=20261015041230. The v is the second Tunarr saved that picture, and it changes only when the picture's bytes do, so Plex and its apps fetch a replaced poster once and can cache the rest for good. Each version stays at its own address for 30 days after it's replaced, so a guide Plex fetched earlier keeps its pictures. A rescan that finds the same picture keeps its address. A poster Tunarr can't save keeps the /api/programs/… address. Pictures no guide has used for 30 days are deleted.

Play your channel by hovering over the channel icon and selecting the play icon.

Warning

Please note, at the time of writing the Plex Windows client is not currently supported and will yield a "This Live TV session has ended" error. Windows users should use the web browser client located at http://serverIP:32400/web until this is resolved. This issue is tracked in chrisbenincasa/tunarr#718

docs.title: Playback
docs.text: Tunarr requires FFmpeg for transcoding / remuxing content when outputting channel streams. Settings relating to transcoding and FFmpeg can be found on the Settings > Playback page (/web/settings/playback). The old /web/settings/ffmpeg address and its transcode-config editor links redirect to Playback.

docs.title: Executable Paths
docs.text:
If Tunarr cannot inspect FFmpeg, capability loading reports an error. Check the configured executable path and its execute permissions before retrying.

Info

Only non-Docker installs must provide FFmpeg executable paths. Docker installs come with a bundled version of FFmpeg.

Configure FFmpeg and FFprobe executable paths. Generally, both executables reside in the same directory. We recommend using a specially built FFmpeg 7.1.1 provided by ErsatzTV.

Above the paths, the page shows the hardware acceleration the configured FFmpeg supports. If Tunarr can't run FFmpeg, a warning appears there instead. Correct the path and save, and Tunarr probes FFmpeg again.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Warn

It is recommended to only enable this setting while debugging. If Tunarr experiences an FFmpeg error, it will still generate an error log file that can be used when troubleshooting issues.

Printing or persisting FFmpeg logs to disk is useful when debugging streaming issues. This setting allows for FFmpeg logging to be outputted to Tunarr's stdout stream or to a separate file with a configurable log level.

docs.title: HLS Direct Output Format
docs.text: When using the HLS Direct stream mode in a channel (see channel stream modes), use this setting to change the output container format for the stream.

docs.title: Scaling and deinterlacing
docs.text: Scaling algorithm selects how FFmpeg resizes video: Bicubic, Fast bilinear, Lanczos, or Spline. Deinterlace filter selects the FFmpeg filter for interlaced video, or None. Both are under Settings > Playback.

docs.title: HDR Tone-map Curve
docs.text:
The curve used to convert HDR programs to SDR when HDR tonemapping is enabled on the software pipeline. It is a matter of taste:

Curve Look Hable (default) Filmic. Keeps detail in shadows and highlights, but darkens the whole picture a little. BT.2390 The ITU broadcast standard. Brighter than Hable, and closer to the source. Möbius Keeps in-range colors as they are and compresses only the brightest highlights. Reinhard A simple, soft curve that can look flat.

The setting takes effect from the next program; no restart is needed. BT.2390 needs an FFmpeg with jellyfin-ffmpeg's tonemapx filter. Other FFmpeg builds use Hable instead.

docs.title: HLS Start-up
docs.text:
These settings trade a little efficiency for a faster tune-in on channels that use the HLS stream mode. They apply when a channel's stream next starts; a stream that is already running keeps its old values.

Setting Default What it does HLS Segment Length (seconds) 4 Length of each HLS segment, with a keyframe at every segment start. Shorter segments are ready sooner; their extra keyframes cost a little picture quality at the same bitrate. HLS Direct (v2) channels copy their source's video and use a fixed four-second target, cutting at source keyframes. Segments Before Playback 2 How many segments must exist before a client gets the playlist. Segment length × this count is roughly the video encoded before the first byte is sent. Tunarr checks for them every 100 ms and waits up to 15 s. MPEG-TS Start-up Burst (seconds) 0 HDHomeRun clients such as Plex read an HLS channel as one .ts stream, made by reading the channel's playlist at real-time pace. With a burst, that reader first sends up to this many seconds of video as fast as it is available, so the client's buffer fills at once. 0 turns it off. Read-ahead Thread Limit 16 While HLS prepares video ahead of playback (the first transcode after a viewer tunes in, or one catching up), it raises the transcode config's thread count up to this limit, and no higher than the CPU cores Tunarr may run on, so the first seconds of video arrive sooner. It never lowers a config's count, and an automatic (0) count stays automatic. 0 turns the increase off. Unlike the settings above, it applies from the next program. See Read-ahead threads.

For example, when the encoder runs near real time, 2 s segments with a 10 s burst send a cold channel's first byte in about half the time of the defaults (4 s instead of 8 s), and fill the client's buffer faster after that.

The served HLS playlist keeps up to 20 segments, with up to 10 segments of history before the playback point. For regular HLS, the default four-second segment length corresponds to roughly an 80-second window and 40-second history; changing HLS Segment Length changes these durations.

HLS Direct v2 uses a fixed four-second target, unaffected by HLS Segment Length. Its copied video can only be cut at source keyframes, so actual segment lengths vary and a 20-segment window does not necessarily span 80 seconds. Alternate HLS also retains its fixed four-second segment configuration.

The playlist FFmpeg writes in the transcode directory (stream.m3u8) holds the last 15 minutes of segments: 225 at the default four seconds, 450 at two. HLS Direct v2 keeps 225, which can span longer when its copied segments do. When TUNARR_SESSION_STALENESS_MS keeps a session nobody watches alive for longer than 10 minutes, the playlist holds that long plus 5 minutes instead. Tunarr keeps the session's history itself, so the playlists it serves count segments and program changes from the start of the session as before. Until 2026-10-19 the file listed every segment since the session started, and FFmpeg rewrote all of it after each segment and read it back in at each program change, which grew costlier the longer a channel played.

HDHomeRun/MPEG-TS tune-ins have a 20-second deadline for their first output byte. A session that exits before producing output fails immediately; a silent startup returns HTTP 504. Disconnecting during startup releases that viewer's connection when session acquisition finishes. An unused timed-out wrapper is retired before another tune. Tune-in logs include session instance IDs, first-byte timing, and the disconnect reason. Debug logs separate channel lock wait, session construction, setup, and readiness. These timings do not include the player's decoding/buffering. FFmpeg and ffprobe version probes are shared and cached by executable path for one hour; failed probes are retried.

docs.title: FFmpeg Transcode Path
docs.text: Configure the path where FFmpeg writes HLS segments for a channel's stream. For instance, if running the standalone Linux binary, Tunarr can write transcoded segments to RAM by setting this option to /dev/shm.

docs.title: Transcode to RAM in Docker
docs.text:
Transcoding to RAM when running Tunarr in Docker requires configuring the container to create a tmpfs at startup time:

docker-compose.yml
# ... rest of your docker compose
services:
    tunarr:
    # ... rest of your Tunarr service
    tmpfs:
        - /transcode:size=10G

Then, in Tunarr, you would set your transcode path to /transcode.

docs.title: Audio & Subtitles
docs.text: These settings are under Settings > Captions & audio, separate from the Playback tab.

docs.title: Subtitle Extraction
docs.text: If content in your channels have embedded, text-based subtitles, this option enables Tunarr to extract subtitles from media files in order to subsequently burn the subtitles. Extract embedded text-based subtitles is currently a requirement for using said subtitle streams. Each hour Tunarr will scan the guide for upcoming media, find which items have embedded text-based subtitles, and then run extraction. This can be a resource-intensive process, so in general, sidecar text-based subtitles are preferable.

docs.title: Sidecar Subtitles
docs.text:
Tunarr supports sidecar subtitle files (.srt, .ass, .ssa and .vtt) placed alongside your media files. When scanning local libraries, Tunarr automatically discovers external subtitle files and associates them with the corresponding media.

In a local library, a subtitle file belongs to a video when it sits in the same folder and its name is the video's name, then the subtitle's language and options, separated by dots:

File Read as Movie (2010).en.srt English Movie (2010).en.sdh.srt English, for the deaf and hard of hearing (also .hi or .cc) Movie (2010).fr.forced.ass French, forced Movie (2010).srt Unknown language

Language codes can be two or three letters (en, eng), with a region (en-us, en_US). The first part that is a language code is the language, so Movie (2010).hi.srt is Hindi, while the .hi in Movie (2010).en.hi.srt means hard of hearing. Subtitle files added after a scan are found at the library's next scan. Versions before 2026-10-16 never found these files; to pick up the ones already on disk in a folder that hasn't changed since, run Force Scan on the library once.

File and folder names may hold any characters, including apostrophes, colons, commas, semicolons, brackets and backslashes. Before 2026-10-17, a subtitle that was burned in (for example a forced one) stopped its program from playing when its path, or for an embedded track the video's path, held an apostrophe, a colon, a comma, a semicolon or a backslash.

For Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby sources, external subtitles are always resolved to a local file during scanning, so that starting a stream never waits on the media server:

  1. Shared storage. If the subtitle file the media server reported is visible to Tunarr — directly, or through the source's path replacements — it is used as-is. Nothing is copied. When a program starts, this file is preferred over any downloaded copy, so a subtitle that was re-synced or replaced on the server is used straight away.
  2. Downloaded during scanning. Otherwise Tunarr fetches the subtitle from the media server and caches it locally.

Setting up path replacements for a media source therefore benefits subtitles as well as video, and is the only way image-based external subtitles can be used, since those cannot be downloaded as text.

Note

Plex reports where a subtitle file is only when Tunarr connects to it through a local address (for example http://127.0.0.1:32400 when both run on the same machine). Through a remote address, such as its plex.direct name, Plex leaves the path out, so Tunarr downloads every subtitle even when it could read the file. A Plex library scan says so in the log once: Plex didn't report subtitle file paths…. Change the Plex server's address under Settings > Media Sources, then run Force Scan on its libraries once.

Every hour, for programs airing in the next hour on channels that have subtitles enabled, Tunarr checks their external subtitles:

  • Missing: a subtitle that could not be resolved during a scan (because the media server was unreachable, for example), or whose cached copy has since been deleted, is fetched, without waiting for a rescan of the whole library.
  • Old copies: a downloaded copy more than 6 hours old is fetched again and replaced only if it changed. The media server can rewrite a subtitle's file under the same stream (a re-sync, a better download). The copy is swapped in whole, so a program that is playing never reads half a file.
  • Gone from the media server: if the media server answers "not found" for a subtitle (its file was replaced or removed), Tunarr reads the program from the media server again at once, saves its subtitles as they are now, and downloads the replacement. It does this once per program per hour. If the media server still lists the subtitle (it hasn't rescanned the item yet), Tunarr keeps what it has until it does. A program the media server no longer has at all is left to the next library scan, which marks it missing.

Note

External subtitles from Jellyfin and Emby libraries scanned by an older version of Tunarr are picked up by that hourly pass once the program is scheduled, or immediately on the next rescan of the library.

When using the HLS Direct v2 stream mode, text-based subtitles (embedded or sidecar files) are served as WebVTT tracks in the HLS master playlist, since this mode can't burn them into the picture. Clients that support HLS subtitle renditions (most modern players) will display them as selectable subtitle options. A channel that starts during a stretch without dialogue starts right away, and its subtitle track stays empty until the next line.

Note

WebVTT subtitle tracks in the HLS stream mode are currently experimental. To enable them, go to Settings > Captions & audio and turn on WebVTT Sidecar Subtitles.

docs.title: Closed Captions for HDHomeRun Clients
docs.text:
Plex Live TV and other HDHomeRun clients read a channel as one MPEG-TS stream. That stream can't carry a selectable subtitle track, so Tunarr normally burns subtitles into the picture. With Closed captions for HDHomeRun clients (Plex) turned on, Tunarr sends them as CEA-608 closed captions instead. Viewers switch them on and off with their player's subtitles or CC button.

When more than 10% of a subtitle track's cues contain characters CEA-608 cannot represent, Tunarr keeps that track for burn-in rather than presenting partial or empty captions. A warning reports the affected cue and character counts. CEA-608 cannot represent Japanese and many other scripts; WebVTT and burn-in do not have that character restriction.

  • Which subtitles: the program's full text subtitles become captions. If the channel's subtitle selection picks forced subtitles (for example, only the foreign-language lines of an English program), those stay burned in, and the program's full subtitles in your preferred language become the captions. Before 2026-10-18, Tunarr read every subtitle track inside a video file as not forced: subtitle selection that asks for forced subtitles never found one, and a forced track (an English dub's "Signs & Songs", say) could become the captions instead of the full one. Tunarr now keeps the flag the media server (or, for a local library, the file) reports, and corrects programs scanned before when it starts.
  • No longer burned in: full text subtitles that would have been burned in for the whole program are sent as captions instead, unless the character-support fallback above requires burn-in, so viewers who want captions must turn them on. Tunarr's own players get them as selectable WebVTT subtitles. Full text subtitles that can't become captions (that fallback, a program whose frame rate is unknown, or a file that can't be read) are burned in even with the WebVTT sidecar option on, so HDHomeRun viewers still see them.
  • Always burned in: image-based subtitles (PGS, VobSub) can't become captions and are still burned in.
  • Requirements: text subtitles on disk, either sidecar files or extracted ones. The channel must use the HLS stream mode and have subtitles enabled, and its transcode config must output H.264 video (its Video Format). The caption track is only added on those channels: on a channel with subtitles off, the .ts stream is left untouched, as with the switch off. Captions can only be added to H.264 video: with HEVC or MPEG-2 output, the whole channel is treated as with the switch off. Its subtitles are burned in as with captions off, programs without subtitles get no notice, and its .ts stream has no caption track. When the channel's .ts stream starts, the log says so once at info level. A channel whose HLS session was started with captions off keeps them off until that session restarts, even after the switch or the channel's subtitles are turned on, and the log says that instead. Before 2026-10-18, such a channel's full text subtitles were neither burned in nor sent as captions. Until 2026-10-19, its .ts stream still offered a caption track that never showed anything.
  • Formatting: italics and underline from the subtitle file (<i>, <u>, and ASS {\i1}, {\u1}) are kept. Other formatting (bold, colors, fonts) is dropped, and so is the text of ASS vector drawings.
  • Placement: captions go where the subtitle file puts them, in a third of the screen: at the top, in the middle or at the bottom, and at the left, centered or at the right. The first of these that a cue has decides:
  • In an ASS file, an exact position (\pos, or where a \move starts): the third of the script's screen it is in.
  • An alignment override in the cue ({\an1} to {\an9}, the numpad layout; or SSA's {\a1} to {\a11}).
  • In an ASS file, the alignment of the cue's style.
  • Otherwise the bottom, centered by Caption Alignment.

Placement and the styles can each be turned off under Caption appearance. - Overlapping subtitles: while two subtitles overlap by more than half a second, both are shown in one block, older above newer (up to 4 lines), at the bottom when the file places them apart. When subtitles overlap under Caption appearance can show each where the file puts it, or only the newest. - Caption Alignment: where lines sit across the screen. Centered block (the default) starts every line in the same column, with the block centered. Each line centered centers each line on its own. Left starts every line at the left edge. - Look: text size and font are the player's, not Tunarr's, and so is the box behind the text unless you choose one under Caption appearance. Plex Live TV (on Apple TV, for example) burns captions into the picture in its own style, a solid dark box behind the text. The text size follows the Plex app's subtitle size setting. In a test, Plex ignored CEA-608's see-through and transparent box codes. - Format limits: lines hold up to 32 characters, two lines at a time (both adjustable under Caption appearance), and long cues are split over time. A style change in the middle of a word takes a column of its own, and so do a text color and a box. Characters outside the caption character set (most non-Latin scripts) are dropped. Accents saved as separate combining marks, as some macOS tools write subtitle files, are joined to their letters first. Before 2026-10-19 such accents were dropped (café became cafe). - Text encoding: a subtitle file that starts with a byte order mark is read as the UTF-8 or UTF-16 it declares. Otherwise it is read as UTF-8 when it is UTF-8 (or nearly all of it is, with a few broken characters), and as Windows-1252, the Western European code page that also covers Latin-1 (ISO 8859-1), when it isn't. Before 2026-10-19, every file was read as UTF-8, so a Windows-1252 file's accented letters were dropped from the captions (café became caf) and a UTF-16 file gave none. A file in another code page (Central European, Cyrillic, Greek) is read as Windows-1252 and its letters come out wrong; save it as UTF-8. Burned-in subtitles are read by ffmpeg, which leaves out any line of a file without a byte order mark that isn't valid UTF-8, so convert such files to UTF-8 to have them burned in. - Every frame carries caption data, even when nothing is being said, so players detect the caption track as soon as they tune in. Each two-character pair is sent once and in order: if a frame is missing where one was due, its pair goes out on the frames that follow instead of being lost. The .ts stream keeps every frame where one segment meets the next and where one program meets the next, so no pair is lost there either. - Frame rate: captions carry two characters per video frame, so while they're on, Tunarr gives each program a fixed, standard output frame rate and lays the captions out at exactly that rate: the program's own (23.976, 25, 29.97...), doubled when the software deinterlacer outputs a frame per field, or 29.97 for a file whose reported rate isn't standard (see Normalize Frame Rate). - Tuning in partway through a subtitle: its caption shows once it has loaded, a fraction of a second in, when at least a second of it is left. A shorter rest is skipped, so the first caption you see is never the end of a line flashing past. Roll-up keeps it, since its lines stay up while the next ones scroll in. - Tuning in while a caption loads: a player that tunes in (Plex reading the stream partway through) can only start decoding at a keyframe, which Tunarr puts at the start of every segment, and Plex's caption decoder starts in roll-up mode. So when a pop-on caption was still loading at that keyframe, the rest of it went straight on screen as a fragment (the end of a line, such as "ng the soup" for "Are you eating the soup?") and could stay up for seconds. Tunarr now loads each caption between two keyframes: before the keyframe when there's room, otherwise just after it, which shows the caption up to 300 ms late. Only when that isn't enough does a caption still load across a keyframe. With 2 s segments and back-to-back dialogue, about 1 tune-in in 60 at 29.97 fps (1 in 16 at 23.976 fps) still meets a fragment, against 1 in 3 before, and 1 caption in 15 to 30 shows later than it did, by 0.15 to 0.2 s typically and never more than 0.3 s. At 59.94 fps nothing moves and no fragment is left. Shorter segments leave less room between keyframes, so more captions load across one. Paint-on and roll-up draw text as it arrives and are unchanged, and so are captions on copied video (HLS Direct v2), whose keyframes Tunarr doesn't know. Hardware encoders can add keyframes of their own (Intel QSV puts one every second), which this doesn't plan around. - Programs without subtitles: players offer captions for the whole stream, so a program with no subtitle track shows a short caption, "No captions for this program", from 1 to 5 seconds into the program (or into the stream, if you tune in partway through), a little later for video below 23.976 fps or when the caption appearance makes it slower to load. A viewer who turns captions on can then tell they work. Filler, flex time and music tracks don't show it, and neither does a program whose subtitles can't become captions (image-based ones are burned in instead). - A program that ends early: when a program's video stops before its scheduled end (FFmpeg exits early, or the file is shorter than its recorded length), its captions stop there too. Before 2026-10-19, an item after it without captions of its own (flex time, an error screen, filler without subtitles) carried the rest of the program's dialogue. A caption still on screen when the program stops is erased where the next item starts. When the next item has captions of its own, the caption stays up until the next item's first caption replaces it. - Language: the stream labels the captions with the first language in your Language Preference, so players such as Plex can name the track by language instead of "Unknown".

docs.title: Caption appearance (experimental)
docs.text:
Everything CEA-608 captions can ask for, under Caption appearance (experimental) below Caption Alignment. A player may ignore any of it: Plex draws captions with its own decoder. Turn on the Test pattern to see what yours shows. Changes take effect from the next program.

To try a look or the test pattern on one channel without changing every channel, use the channel's own caption settings, then Copy to all channels once the look works.

  • Text color: white, green, blue, cyan, red, yellow or magenta. Italic words are always white, which is how CEA-608 defines italics.
  • Box behind the text: the player's own (the default: Tunarr sends nothing), or black, white, green, blue, cyan, red, yellow or magenta. Box opacity makes a chosen box solid, see-through, or none at all (the text alone). The box holds to the end of every line: Plex's family of caption decoders turns the box back to black when the previous caption is cleared, so Tunarr loads each boxed line wholly before or after that clear (test pattern sample 39). In very quick dialogue, where a caption only just loads in time, Tunarr keeps the caption on time instead, and the end of a line can still lose its box.
  • How captions appear: Pop-on (the default) shows each caption whole, on its start frame. Roll-up scrolls lines up from the bottom row with 2, 3 or 4 rows on screen, as live TV captions do; a cue's lines stay together, and the last lines stay up for up to 2 seconds for the next subtitle to scroll. Paint-on draws each caption's letters as they arrive.
  • Lines per caption: 2 (the default), 3 or 4. More lines split long subtitles less often. Roll-up uses its own number of rows.
  • Line width: 20 to 32 columns. A narrower line wraps sooner.
  • Bottom row and Top row: the screen has 15 caption rows. Captions end on the bottom row (15, the default); captions the subtitle file places at the top start on the top row (1), and ones it places in the middle sit between the two.
  • When subtitles overlap: Show both, stacked (the default) puts both in one block, older above newer; when the file places them apart (a sign at the top over dialogue), the block goes at the bottom, because Plex's family of caption decoders positions only a caption's first line. Show each where the subtitle file puts it keeps them apart, for players that place every line (test pattern sample 38 shows whether yours does). Show the newest shows one at a time, bringing the earlier back when the newer ends if it lasts at least another second. Roll-up and paint-on always show one at a time.
  • All capitals, and whether to keep the subtitle file's italics and underline and its placement (top, middle and sides).

A box, a color or narrower lines make each caption take longer to send, so in fast dialogue a caption can come a little late. Roll-up and paint-on send a caption's text while it is on screen, at two characters a frame, so a long caption with a short time is cut off at its end.

Test pattern: replaces every program's captions with 39 numbered samples that loop, one per feature, each saying what it should look like. Turn captions on in your player, note the numbers that look wrong, then turn the test pattern off. Your appearance settings don't change the samples. A channel's own Test pattern on this channel switch shows it on that channel only.

# Sample 1–7 Text colors: white, green, blue, cyan, red, yellow, magenta 8 Red text with white italics in the middle 9, 10 Italics, underline 11–18 Boxes: black, red, green, blue, cyan, magenta, then blue text on yellow and on white 19, 20 See-through black and blue boxes 21 No box at all 22–25 Rows 1 and 5 (top), 11 and 13 (bottom) 26, 27 Three and four lines 28, 29 Left-aligned lines, and each line centered 30 Flashing text 31 Paint-on 32–34 Roll-up with 2, 3 and 4 rows 35 Middle of the screen 36 Right-aligned 37 Two overlapping lines, stacked 38 A sign at the top and a line at the bottom at once, each in its place 39 A magenta box, then a second line straight after it that keeps the magenta box to its last character (italics and ♪ included)

The setting takes effect from the next program, and the HDHomeRun stream picks it up the next time it is started.

docs.title: Language Preference
docs.text:
Currently, language preferences can only be configured globally. Use this setting to set an ordered list of preferred audio languages. The first matching audio language stream for a given piece of content will be chosen.

Note

ISO 639-2 gives 20 languages two different three-letter codes — German is both ger and deu, French both fre and fra — and media servers and files use them interchangeably. Tunarr treats the two codes for a language as equivalent, so a preference matches a track regardless of which code the file or media server reports.

docs.title: Transcode Configs
docs.text:
Transcode Configurations provide Tunarr with a set of parameters to produce a normalized output stream for a given channel. These configurations are responsible for options like hardware acceleration, output video/audio formats, bit rates, and more. Transcode configurations are applied per-channel and can be shared across multiple channels. This page explores each option in detail.

Save is available once something has changed. Saving a new configuration opens it for editing, and leaving the page with unsaved changes asks first.

Performance: Hardware Acceleration Strongly Recommended

Software transcoding (Hardware Acceleration = None) is extremely CPU-intensive. Transcoding even a single 1080p stream can saturate multiple CPU cores, and on modest or low-power hardware (NAS devices, Raspberry Pi, older PCs) it will cause dropped frames, stuttering, or an inability to keep up with real-time playback.

Hardware-accelerated encoding is strongly recommended for most users. See Hardware Acceleration below to find the right mode for your system.

docs.title: General Settings
docs.text:
• Name — A human-readable label for this configuration. Used to identify the config when assigning it to a channel.
  • Thread Count — CPU threads available to FFmpeg for software encoding and decoding. Set to 0 for automatic selection. Real-time transcodes use this count; HLS can temporarily increase it while preparing video ahead of playback (see Read-ahead threads). Hardware pipelines can still use CPU threads for software filters and fallback encoding.
  • Disable watermarks — When enabled, suppresses the channel watermark/logo overlay for streams using this configuration. Useful if you want a clean output without branding.

docs.title: Read-ahead threads
docs.text: Transcoding settings include Read-ahead Thread Limit (default 16). HLS may raise the configured thread count up to this limit while preparing video ahead of playback, subject to available CPU cores. It never lowers the transcode configuration's own count. Set the limit to 0 to disable this increase; a configuration using automatic threads remains automatic. Changes apply from the next program. The limit is useful for controlling the temporary increase; it does not cap FFmpeg’s total thread usage. Software HEVC encoding also passes the chosen count to x265's worker pool.

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
Configure output video parameters including hardware acceleration, format, resolution, and bitrate.

Video options, captured 2026-10-21 from source f837ef4c.

docs.title: Hardware Acceleration
docs.text:
Hardware acceleration offloads video encoding and decoding from the CPU to dedicated hardware (GPU or media engine), dramatically reducing CPU usage and allowing real-time transcoding on modest hardware.

Mode Platform Tonemapping When to Use None Any Software Software-only transcoding. CPU-intensive. Only use if no hardware acceleration is available or for debugging. CUDA NVIDIA GPUs (Linux/Windows) Hardware (Vulkan) / Software fallback Requires an NVIDIA GPU with NVENC support. The most reliable hardware path on Linux and Windows with NVIDIA hardware. VAAPI Intel / AMD GPUs (Linux) tonemap_vaapi / tonemap_opencl / Software fallback Uses the Video Acceleration API. Defaults to /dev/dri/renderD128. Supported drivers: system, ihd, i965, radeonsi, nouveau. Recommended for Intel and AMD users on Linux. QSV Intel GPUs (Linux/Windows) Hardware (experimental) Intel Quick Sync Video. Cannot hardware-decode 10-bit H.264 or HEVC content. Generally less stable than VAAPI on Linux; may work well on Windows. VideoToolbox macOS Not supported Apple's hardware video codec framework. Works on both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs. Recommended for all macOS users.

Linux with Intel GPU: VAAPI vs QSV

If you are running Tunarr on Linux with an Intel GPU, VAAPI is the recommended choice over QSV. VAAPI is generally more stable, better tested with Tunarr. QSV may work for some users but can produce compatibility issues with certain codecs and bit depths.

When VAAPI or QSV is selected, the device path option appears:

  • VAAPI Device Path — Path to the DRI render device (default: /dev/dri/renderD128). Change this only if your device is at a non-standard path (e.g., /dev/dri/renderD129 when multiple GPUs are present).

The VAAPI driver is stored as vaapiDriver in the transcode configuration and defaults to system; the form does not expose a driver selector.

When VAAPI is selected, Tunarr will automatically use hardware-accelerated pad filters (pad_vaapi, or pad_opencl as a fallback) for letterboxing and pillarboxing operations. This keeps padding on the GPU and avoids a round-trip to software. If your hardware does not support these filters or you observe artifacts, you can force software padding by setting TUNARR_DISABLE_VAAPI_PAD=true.

docs.title: Video Format
docs.text:
Controls the codec used to encode the output video stream.

  • H.264 (AVC) — The most compatible format, supported by virtually all clients and devices. A safe default for most setups.
  • HEVC (H.265) — Better compression than H.264 at equivalent quality, meaning lower bitrates for the same visual quality. However, encoding is more computationally expensive, and not all clients support HEVC playback. Recommended only if your clients support it and you have capable hardware.
  • MPEG-2 — A legacy format with the highest compatibility but the least efficient compression. Only use this if you have specific clients that require it.

docs.title: Video Preset
docs.text:
Software H.264 and HEVC encoding offers ultrafast, superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium, slow, slower, and veryslow. The default is veryfast. Slower presets spend more CPU time compressing each frame; check that the encoder can still keep up with live playback.

HLS and HLS Alt streams keep their starting configuration until everyone stops watching and the stream restarts. HLS Direct and MPEG-TS streams pick up a changed preset from the next program.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Sets the output resolution as width × height. Tunarr will scale the source video to this resolution. Available presets range from 420×420 to 3840×2160 (4K UHD), with 1920×1080 (Full HD) as a reasonable default for most setups.

Warning

Higher resolutions significantly increase the load on both the encoder and any connected hardware. Transcoding 4K content in software is not feasible on most hardware. Even with hardware acceleration, ensure your GPU supports encoding at the target resolution before selecting 4K.

docs.title: Video Bitrate
docs.text:
The target output bitrate for the video stream, in kilobits per second (kbps). FFmpeg uses this as a target and may produce slightly higher or lower bitrates depending on scene complexity.

  • Default: 2000 kbps — Suitable for 720p content
  • For 1080p, 4000–8000 kbps is a common range
  • For 4K, 15000–25000 kbps is typical

Lower bitrates reduce file size and network usage but decrease visual quality. Higher bitrates improve quality at the cost of bandwidth and storage.

docs.title: Video Buffer Size
docs.text:
Controls how frequently FFmpeg re-evaluates the output bitrate, in kilobits. A larger buffer allows more bitrate variation over a short period; a smaller buffer enforces stricter bitrate compliance.

A common starting point is roughly 2× the video bitrate (e.g., 4000 kb buffer for a 2000 kbps target). Increase the buffer if you notice bitrate spikes causing buffering; decrease it for more consistent network usage.

docs.title: Normalize Frame Rate
docs.text:
When enabled, forces the output stream to a consistent frame rate (e.g., 23.976, 29.97, or 60 fps). This is recommended for most setups, as mixing frame rates across lineup items can cause playback issues or stuttering with some clients.

A source whose file reports a frame rate that isn't a standard one (23.976, 24, 25, 29.97, 30, 50, 59.94 or 60) always gets a rate that holds every frame, with this setting on or off: 29.97, or 59.94 if it reports more than 30 fps. Some DVD rips report 20 fps for video whose frames really come 24 or 30 a second; kept at 20, about one frame in six was dropped. A rate up to 2% below a standard one counts as that rate (23.81 is treated as 23.976), and so does a rounded label (23.98); a rate a little above a standard one doesn't, since rounding it down would drop frames. A rate above 60 (high-frame-rate video, such as 120) is kept as reported.

docs.title: Deinterlace Video
docs.text: Applies a deinterlace filter to the output. Enable this if your source content is interlaced — common with recordings from broadcast or cable TV. The specific deinterlace filter used is configured globally, as ffmpeg.deinterlaceFilter in settings.json (the settings page doesn't show it yet). This setting has no effect on progressive (non-interlaced) source content.

docs.title: HDR Tonemapping
docs.text:
Experimental

HDR tonemapping is an experimental feature. Results may vary depending on hardware, driver version, and source content. It may cause stream errors on some configurations. Monitor logs closely when first enabling it.

When Tunarr encounters HDR content (HDR10 or HLG), it can convert it to SDR during transcoding. This is useful when playback devices or clients do not support HDR, or when a consistent SDR output is required regardless of source content.

Tonemapping is disabled by default. To enable it, set the TUNARR_TONEMAP_ENABLED environment variable (see Environment Variables).

When enabled, Tunarr automatically selects the best available tonemapping method for the configured hardware acceleration mode:

Hardware Mode Method Notes VAAPI tonemap_opencl → tonemap_vaapi → software Tunarr uses tonemap_opencl only when FFmpeg can create an OpenCL device from the VAAPI device. It tests this when it first detects VAAPI capabilities. If the test fails (common on Intel iGPUs whose OpenCL runtime lacks VAAPI sharing, and on all AMD GPUs), Tunarr uses tonemap_vaapi, then software. CUDA Hardware tonemapping via Vulkan Requires Vulkan support on the host. If Vulkan is unavailable or causing stream errors, set TUNARR_DISABLE_VULKAN=true to fall back to software tonemapping. QSV Hardware tonemapping Experimental. May not work reliably on all hardware. None (Software) tonemapx → zscale + tonemap Used as the final fallback for all modes. More CPU-intensive than hardware paths. Tunarr uses tonemapx, a much faster SIMD tone mapper, when the FFmpeg build has it (jellyfin-ffmpeg does); otherwise zscale with FFmpeg's tonemap filter. Either way the HDR10 metadata is removed from the SDR output. The curve is set with HDR Tone-map Curve in Transcoding settings (see FFmpeg).

Tonemapping is only applied to content Tunarr identifies as HDR (HDR10 or HLG). SDR content is unaffected.

Color Metadata

Tonemapping relies on color metadata (color space, color transfer, color primaries) stored in Tunarr's database for each program. This metadata is populated automatically when media is scanned or imported from a media source. If tonemapping is not being applied to content you expect to be HDR, try re-scanning the relevant library to ensure the metadata has been recorded.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Configure output audio parameters including codec, channels, bitrate, and volume.

Audio options, captured 2026-10-21 from source f837ef4c.

docs.title: Audio Format
docs.text:
Controls the codec used to encode the output audio stream.

  • AAC — The default and most compatible format. Widely supported by all clients and streaming devices. Recommended for most setups.
  • AC3 (Dolby Digital) — Good choice for surround sound (5.1) content. Supported by most TVs and AV receivers, but not all streaming clients.
  • E-AC3 (Dolby Digital Plus) — Supports higher bitrates and more channels than AC3 but is less supported. Use if you want to stream 7.1 (8 channel) surround sound and have compatible clients/hardware.
  • Opus (experimental) — Highly efficient compression with inexpensive transcode perfomance and better multi-channel support than AAC or MP3. Would be ideal for surround sound content except that it isn't officially part of the the HLS spec as it is unsupported by most A/V hardware. Offered as an experimental option as it may still function due to nearly-universal software support.
  • MP3 — Widely compatible but lower quality than AAC at equivalent bitrates. Only use if a specific client requires it.
  • Copy — Passes the audio stream through unchanged without re-encoding. When Copy is selected, all other audio settings (bitrate, sample rate, volume, channels) are ignored, since the stream is not being processed by FFmpeg.

docs.title: Audio Channels
docs.text:
The number of output audio channels as a whole integer. Common values:

  • 2 — Stereo
  • 6 — 5.1 surround
  • 8 — 7.1 surround

docs.title: Audio Bitrate
docs.text: The target output bitrate for the audio stream, in kilobits per second (kbps). For AAC stereo, 128–192 kbps is a common range. For AC3 5.1 surround, 384–640 kbps is typical.

docs.title: Audio Buffer Size
docs.text: Controls how frequently FFmpeg re-evaluates the audio bitrate, in kilobits. Analogous to the video buffer size setting. A value of roughly 2× the audio bitrate is a reasonable starting point.

docs.title: Audio Sample Rate
docs.text: The output sample rate in Hz. The default of 48000 Hz (48 kHz) is standard for video content and recommended for most setups. Changing this is rarely necessary.

docs.title: Audio Volume %
docs.text:
Adjusts the output volume relative to the source.

  • 100 — Original volume (no change)
  • Values above 100 amplify the audio (e.g., 150 = 50% louder)
  • Values below 100 attenuate the audio (e.g., 80 = 20% quieter)

Info

This setting has no effect when Audio Format is set to Copy, since the audio stream is passed through without processing.

docs.title: Loudness Normalization
docs.text:
Tunarr supports EBU R128 loudness normalization via FFmpeg's loudnorm filter. This provides more perceptually consistent loudness leveling across different programs, compared to the simple volume percentage adjustment above.

When enabled, the following parameters can be configured:

Parameter Range Default Description Integrated Loudness (I) -70.0 to -5.0 LUFS -24.0 Target integrated loudness. EBU R128 broadcast standard is -23 LUFS; -24 is a common streaming target. Loudness Range (LRA) 1.0 to 50.0 LU 7.0 Target loudness range (dynamic range). Lower values compress dynamics more aggressively. Max True Peak (TP) -9.0 to 0.0 dBTP -2.0 Maximum allowed true peak level, preventing clipping.

Loudness normalization and Audio Volume % can be used independently of each other.

Info

Loudness normalization has no effect when Audio Format is set to Copy, since the audio stream is passed through without processing.

docs.title: Advanced Options
docs.text:
Warning

Do not change these settings unless you understand their implications. These are diagnostic and compatibility options intended for troubleshooting, not normal operation.

  • Disable Hardware Decoding — Forces FFmpeg to use software (CPU) decoding even when a hardware acceleration mode is selected. Hardware encoding will still be used if enabled. This is useful when the hardware decoder is incompatible with a specific source format or bit depth (e.g., 10-bit H.264 with QSV).

  • Disable Hardware Encoding — Forces FFmpeg to use software (CPU) encoding even when a hardware acceleration mode is selected. Hardware decoding will still be used if enabled. This can be used to debug quality issues or when the hardware encoder produces artifacts on specific content.

  • Disable Hardware Filters — Forces CPU-based filters (scaling, deinterlacing, overlays) even when hardware acceleration is enabled. Normally, filters are applied on the GPU for efficiency. Enable this if hardware filter compatibility causes issues with your setup.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Configure how Tunarr responds when a transcoding error occurs — for example, when a source file is missing or a media server is unreachable.

Info

More configurable error options are tracked in chrisbenincasa/tunarr#1292

Error options, captured 2026-10-21 from source f837ef4c.

docs.title: Error Video Mode
docs.text:
Controls what appears on screen when a transcoding error occurs:

  • pic — Displays a placeholder image (default). A static error image is shown for the duration of the errored item.
  • blank — Outputs a blank (black) screen with no video content.
  • static — Outputs TV-style static/noise.
  • testsrc — Outputs color bars with a timer, similar to a test pattern broadcast.
  • text — Displays a text message. Requires the FFmpeg drawtext filter to be available.
  • kill — Stops the stream entirely when an error occurs. The session will terminate rather than playing an error placeholder.

docs.title: Error Audio Mode
docs.text:
Controls what audio plays during a transcoding error:

  • whitenoise — Plays white noise audio.
  • sine — Plays a repeating sine wave tone (beep).
  • silent — No audio during error periods.

Automatic Retry
