docs.title: Slot Linking
docs.text: Slot linking lets you tie two or more slots together so they share a single episode iterator. Without linking, every slot maintains its own independent position in its program list. With linking, the connected slots advance through their content as a group.

docs.title: Default Behavior: Isolated Slots
docs.text:
By default, every slot is isolated. Even if two slots reference the same show, each one keeps its own cursor. Consider a schedule with two slots that both play Seinfeld:

Slot Show Order A Seinfeld Next B Seinfeld Next

Without linking, each slot independently walks through the episode list. Slot A plays S01E01, then S01E02 the next time it is chosen. Slot B also starts at S01E01 and advances on its own. The two never coordinate, so duplicate episodes are likely.

This isolation is intentional. It means adding a second slot for the same content is always safe and predictable -- it will not interfere with any other slot's progress.

docs.title: Linking Slots Together
docs.text:
To link slots, open a slot's edit dialog and use the Link to existing slot control. When you link slot B to slot A:

  1. Both slots are assigned to the same iteration group (a shared UUID).
  2. Slot B adopts the content configuration (show, ordering, direction, filler, mid-roll) of slot A.
  3. Both slots now share one program iterator.

You can link more than two slots to the same group. All members of a group must reference the same content source and use the same ordering.

docs.title: What Gets Shared
docs.text:
When slots are linked, the following fields are copied from the source slot and kept in sync across the group:

  • Content source (show, movie pool, custom show, or smart collection)
  • Ordering (next, shuffle, chronological, etc.)
  • Direction (ascending / descending)
  • Filler configuration
  • Mid-roll break configuration

docs.title: What Stays Independent
docs.text:
Each slot retains its own:

  • Slot duration or start time
  • Weight (in random/weighted mode)
  • Cooldown
  • Padding overrides

docs.title: Link Modes
docs.text: Once slots are linked, you choose a link mode that controls how the shared iterator advances.

docs.title: Continue (default)
docs.text:
In continue mode, linked slots advance the shared iterator sequentially. Each time any slot in the group plays, it picks up where the previous one left off.

Example with two linked Seinfeld slots in continue mode:

Turn Slot Chosen Episode Played 1 A S01E01 2 B S01E02 3 A S01E03 4 B S01E04

This is useful for spreading a single show across multiple time slots or schedule positions while ensuring every episode airs exactly once before the list wraps around.

docs.title: Rerun
docs.text:
In rerun mode, the shared iterator only advances after every slot in the group has played the current episode. Each member of the group plays the same episode, and the group advances together.

Example with two linked Seinfeld slots in rerun mode:

Turn Slot Chosen Episode Played 1 A S01E01 2 B S01E01 3 A S01E02 4 B S01E02

This mimics the "rerun" pattern of traditional TV where the same episode airs at different times of day (e.g. a primetime airing and a late-night repeat).

docs.title: Validation Rules
docs.text:
Tunarr validates linked slot groups when you save a schedule. The following rules are enforced:

  • Consistent content: All slots in a group must reference the same content source and ordering. Mismatched content keys produce an error.
  • Consistent link mode: All slots in a group must use the same link mode. You cannot mix continue and rerun within a single group.
  • Orphaned link mode: If a slot has a link mode set but no iteration group (i.e. it is not linked to anything), the link mode is silently stripped during validation.

docs.title: Linkable Slot Types
docs.text:
Not all slot types support linking. The following slot types can be linked:

Slot Type Linkable Movie Yes Show Yes Custom Show Yes Smart Collection Yes Filler No Flex No Redirect No

Filler, flex, and redirect slots do not maintain program iterators in the same way, so linking does not apply to them.

docs.title: Unlinking
docs.text:
To remove a slot from its group, open the slot's edit dialog and click Unlink. This clears the slot's iteration group and link mode, returning it to the default isolated behavior. The remaining group members are unaffected.

If you unlink all members of a group (leaving only one), that last slot continues to function normally as an isolated slot.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Avoid accidental duplicates: If you have two unlinked slots for the same show and want them to coordinate, link them. Otherwise they will independently iterate through the same episode list.
  • Continue mode for coverage: Use continue mode when you want to spread a show across multiple schedule positions and play every episode once.
  • Rerun mode for repetition: Use rerun mode when you want the same episode to air in multiple slots before moving on, simulating same-day reruns.
  • Order matters for rerun: In rerun mode, the iterator advances after the entire group has consumed the current item. The order in which slots are chosen does not affect which episode plays -- all group members see the same one until they have all played it.

docs.title: Time Slots
docs.text:
Time Slots allow you to schedule specific shows to run at specific time slots each day or week.

To schedule Time Slots for your channel programming, select "TOOLS", then "Time Slots".

In this example, we want "Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters" to always air at 10am each day, followed by "Batman Beyond" at 10:30am each day. We also want Flex to fill the time in-between episodes using the Pad Times option, so that episodes always air right at 10am and 10:30am. We have allowed 5 minutes of lateness, so if an episode runs over the 30 minute time slot by 5 minutes or less, the next shows episode will still play no later than 10:35am.

Save is enabled once a slot or setting has changed, or after "Refresh Preview" made a new lineup. "Reset changes" puts back the saved slots and lineup, and leaving the editor with unsaved changes asks first.

See below for an example of our current schedule. Please note that as we have only selected two time slots for the entire day, "Batman Beyond" being our last scheduled show will continue airing until the following day at 10am when the next scheduled episode of "Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters" is set to air.

If we instead wanted to air these two episodes, then have the channel play Flex content until the next episode of "Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters" the following day at 10am, we would simply add Flex after "Batman Beyond".

See below for an example of our schedule now that we have Flex after our two episodes air. Now it will alternate Show 1 Day 1, Show 2 Day 1, Show 1 Day 2, Show 2 Day 2, etc.

docs.title: Slot Requirements
docs.text:
Tunarr checks these rules when you save or preview a schedule, and rejects a schedule that breaks one with HTTP 400.

  • A schedule needs at least one slot.
  • Each slot's start time is a whole number of milliseconds within the period.
  • Pad times and the number of days to schedule are greater than zero.
  • Every filler list, show, smart collection, and channel a slot references must exist.

docs.title: Empty or Deleted Custom Shows
docs.text:
A custom show with no programs cannot fill a time slot.

  • The editor does not offer empty custom shows for new slots.
  • A saved slot whose custom show later becomes empty, or is deleted, keeps its selection and shows a warning. Choose another show or remove the slot. Saving is blocked until every slot is fixed.
  • The API rejects a new schedule or preview that references an empty or unknown custom show with HTTP 400, and leaves the channel's lineup unchanged.
  • When Tunarr regenerates an already saved schedule, the empty slot's time is filled with Flex.
  • Programs with no duration are skipped, because they cannot advance the schedule.

docs.title: Slot Linking
docs.text:
By default, each time slot maintains its own episode cursor. If the same show appears in multiple time slots (e.g. a morning and evening airing), each slot independently starts at episode 1 and advances separately.

To make multiple time slots share a single episode iterator, use Slot Linking. In continue mode, the slots advance together sequentially. In rerun mode, every linked slot plays the same episode before the group moves on -- useful for simulating same-day reruns at different times.

docs.title: Padding
docs.text: Padding controls how Tunarr handles the gap between when a program finishes and when the next scheduled slot is due to start. When a program ends before its slot's start time, Tunarr fills the gap with Flex content (or silence if no filler is configured) so that the next program begins at exactly the scheduled time.

docs.title: Global Pad Time
docs.text: The Pad Times setting applies a uniform pad duration to all slots in the schedule. This is the primary way to enforce "hard" start times: if an episode finishes 8 minutes before the next slot, those 8 minutes are filled with flex content.

docs.title: Per-Slot Padding
docs.text:
Individual slots can override the global pad time with their own value. This is useful when different slots have different tolerance requirements — for example, a morning block that needs tight padding while an evening block can be more flexible.

To set per-slot padding, open the slot's options in the Time Slot editor. When a slot has its own pad time set, it takes precedence over the global Pad Times value for that slot only. Slots without a per-slot override continue to use the global value.

docs.title: Max Lateness
docs.text:
The Max Lateness setting is a companion to padding. It defines how late a slot may start when the program before it runs long. Tunarr never cuts a program off, so a program that runs past the next slot's start time always plays in full. When it ends, Tunarr checks how late the slot it has run into would start:

  • If the slot would start within its max lateness, it starts late.
  • Otherwise Tunarr skips that slot, fills the rest of its time with Flex, and resumes at the next slot's start time.

For example, with a max lateness of 5 minutes, an episode that ends 4 minutes into the next slot is followed by that slot's program, 4 minutes late. An episode that ends 6 minutes into the next slot is followed by Flex until the slot after it begins.

A slot can override the global max lateness in its options in the Time Slot editor. The override applies when Tunarr arrives late at that slot, so set it on the slot that would be delayed or skipped, not on the slot that runs long.

docs.title: Example: A Long Program in a Short Slot
docs.text:
An anime slot airs 22-minute episodes in a 30-minute slot at 6:00pm, and the season ends with a 100-minute movie. The global pad time is 5 minutes. On the movie's day:

  1. The movie plays in full, from 6:00pm to 7:40pm.
  2. Any slot that starts and ends while the movie is playing, like a 6:30pm slot, is skipped for that day.
  3. The 7:30pm slot is 10 minutes late when the movie ends. With the global max lateness at 5 minutes, Tunarr skips it and plays Flex until the next slot. If the 7:30pm slot has its own max lateness of 15 minutes, its program starts at 7:40pm instead.

The global max lateness can stay small, because the long program never needs lateness to finish. Pad time is applied before lateness, so with a 30-minute global pad time Tunarr would first fill 7:40pm to 8:00pm with Flex and the 7:30pm slot would never be considered.

docs.title: Max Overflow
docs.text:
The Max Overflow setting controls how many programs a slot packs in. A slot always plays at least one program. After that, Tunarr keeps adding programs from the slot while they fit:

  • Do not allow adds a program only if it ends by the next slot's start time.
  • A duration such as 15 minutes lets an added program end up to that long after the next slot's start time.
  • One extra item keeps adding programs until the slot is full, so the last one may run past the next slot's start time by any amount.

Max overflow and max lateness work together. Overflow decides how far a slot may run past its end, and the next slot's max lateness decides whether that slot then starts late or is skipped. Like max lateness, overflow can be set globally or overridden per slot.

docs.title: When settings take effect
docs.text:
Timing chips describe when saved settings are read. Live means Tunarr reads the setting without a restart; it does not interrupt work already running. Next program means a new program pipeline, which may already be preparing ahead of playback. Next session means the channel must stop streaming before it starts again; stop all viewers first. Reload required means reload the browser page. Restart required means restart the Tunarr server.

Browser preferences apply as they change. The server address is stored in this browser when you select Save, even if the server settings request fails; reload the page to use it. Server-managed controls apply after a successful save. Environment overrides still take precedence over saved settings.

Setting or group Applies Details Browser preferences Live Changes apply in this browser as you make them. Server address Reload required Reload this browser page after saving the server address so all API clients connect to the saved server. Server port Restart required Restart Tunarr to listen on the saved port. Base logging and log rotation Live Saving updates the base log level and rotation rules immediately. Category log level Live Saving an explicit category log level updates that category immediately. Inherited category log level Restart required Returning a category from an explicit level to Inherit requires restarting Tunarr, unless changing the base log level or rotation settings also rebuilds the loggers. Backup configuration and schedules Live Saving replaces the backup schedules immediately. A backup already running keeps its original output options. Search indexing Restart required Restart Tunarr to relaunch Meilisearch with the saved snapshot interval and memory limit. Environment overrides still take precedence. Library scan interval Live Saving reschedules library scans and collection and custom-show syncs immediately. A scan already running continues. FFmpeg and FFprobe executable paths Next program New probes and processes use the saved executable paths. Processes already running continue with their original binaries. FFmpeg logging Next program New program FFmpeg processes use the saved logging destination and level. Processes already running keep their logging options. HLS Direct output format Next program New HLS Direct playlists and program streams use the saved container format. A stream already running keeps its original format. Video scaling, deinterlacing and tone mapping Next program The next program pipeline reads the saved scaling, deinterlace and tone-map settings. A program already transcoding keeps its pipeline. HLS read-ahead thread limit Next program The next HLS program transcode reads the saved read-ahead thread limit. A transcode already running keeps its thread count. HLS segments and startup buffering Next session New HLS sessions read the saved segment length and initial segment count. New MPEG-TS wrapper sessions read the startup burst. FFmpeg transcode path Next session New sessions write to the saved directory. Existing sessions keep writing to their original directory until they end. Embedded subtitle extraction Live Enabling starts an extraction run immediately. Disabling is checked before each queued program; an extraction already running can finish. HDHomeRun closed captions Next session Caption delivery is fixed when an HLS session starts. Stop all viewers of the channel and tune in again to change it. Caption alignment, appearance and test pattern Next program The next program pipeline reads the saved caption style and test pattern. A program already transcoding keeps its captions. Global subtitle preferences Next program Future stream selections on inheriting channels use the saved subtitle preferences. A program already streaming keeps its selected subtitles. Audio language preferences Next program The next program pipeline selects audio using the saved language preferences. Transcode configurations Next session Active HLS sessions retain their channel transcode configuration. Stop all viewers of the channel and tune in again to use an edited configuration. Guide settings Live Saving reschedules guide refreshes and rebuilds the guide immediately using the saved settings. HDHomeRun network discovery Restart required Restart Tunarr to start or stop HDHomeRun discovery advertising. HDHomeRun tuner count Live New HDHomeRun discovery and device-information responses report the saved tuner count. Clients may need to refresh the device. Proxy artwork Live New artwork requests use the saved flag. Images already loaded by a client may remain cached. HDR tonemapping feature Next program The next program pipeline reads this flag. A pipeline already running keeps its tone-mapping behavior. WebVTT sidecar subtitles Next program The next program pipeline reads this flag when preparing subtitle outputs. XMLTV credit images Live Guide writers read this flag on each write. Regenerate the guide to update existing XMLTV output. Search snapshot in backups Live New backup archives read this flag. A backup already running can keep its original snapshot behavior. Disable Vulkan Next program The next NVIDIA program pipeline reads this flag. A pipeline already running is unchanged. Disable VAAPI padding Next program The next VAAPI program pipeline reads this flag. A pipeline already running is unchanged.

docs.title: Captions & audio
docs.text:
Choose subtitle handling, caption appearance, and preferred audio languages under Settings > Captions & audio (/web/settings/captions-audio).

This tab contains global subtitle preferences, embedded subtitle extraction, HDHomeRun closed captions, caption alignment and appearance, and preferred input audio languages. See Audio & Subtitles for details.

The optional WebVTT Sidecar Subtitles feature is also here, with its own Save button. This feature keeps its own enablement control; subtitle preferences do not turn it on.

Closed-caption delivery is fixed when the channel's HLS session starts. Stop all viewers and tune in again after changing that switch. Caption alignment, appearance, test pattern and audio language preferences are read by the next program pipeline. See when settings take effect for every group.

docs.title: Global subtitle preferences
docs.text:
Add languages in the order Tunarr should try them. Each row has its own filter (Any, Forced, Default or None) and controls for external and image-based subtitles. Move rows to change priority, remove a row or clear the list, then Save. Reset changes discards unsaved edits.

Channels using global preferences follow this list. A nonempty list with no matching row selects no subtitle; None skips that row. An empty global list keeps the stream mode's existing fallback. These preferences do not enable subtitles, extraction, captions or WebVTT output. HLS Direct v2 can only use text subtitles. A program already streaming keeps its selected subtitles.

Choose Customize for this channel on a channel's Streaming tab for an exception. Returning to global preferences retains its custom list for later. Fixed output audio tracks remain a per-channel choice; the input audio language preference list on this page does not create an output track layout.

View global and channel screenshots.

docs.title: Experimental
docs.text:
Try optional features and work around server issues under Settings > Experimental (/web/settings/experimental). The old /web/settings/features address redirects here.

This tab contains Proxy Artwork, XMLTV Credit Images, and Disable Search Snapshot in Backup. Playback options (HDR Tonemapping, Disable Vulkan, and Disable VAAPI Pad) are under Settings > Playback. WebVTT Sidecar Subtitles is under Settings > Captions & audio.

Flags set by environment variables are read-only and marked on the page. Moving a flag to another tab does not change what it does or when it applies.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Manage web preferences, server access, logging, and backups under Settings > General (/web/settings/general). Opening Settings goes here.

Web preferences apply in this browser. The server form has its own Save and Reset changes controls. See Logging and Backup & Restore for details.

See when settings take effect for the timing shown by settings chips.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text:
Configure XMLTV guide output and refreshes under Settings > Guide (/web/settings/guide). The old /web/settings/xmltv address redirects here.

Set the output path, guide length, refresh interval, and picture address here. You can also refresh or download the guide. See Channel Guide for guide URLs and how channel settings affect the output.

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
Configure library scans and search indexing under Settings > Library (/web/settings/library). The old /web/settings/scanner address redirects here.

The rescan interval applies when saved, and the page shows the next scheduled scan. See Scheduled Scans for timing and related collection syncs. Manage connections separately under Sources.

docs.title: Search indexing
docs.text:
Search snapshot interval (hours) sets how often Meilisearch saves its index snapshot. Indexing memory limit (bytes) sets the memory budget for indexing; leave it empty to use Meilisearch's default. Both settings show Restart required because Tunarr passes them to Meilisearch at startup. The scan interval still applies immediately.

TUNARR_SEARCH_MAX_MEMORY takes precedence over the saved memory limit. The setting is stored in bytes, as described in the Meilisearch configuration reference.

docs.title: Tuner
docs.text:
Manage HDHomeRun discovery and tuner capacity under Settings > Tuner (/web/settings/tuner). The old /web/settings/hdhr address redirects here.

Network discovery announces Tunarr to clients on your network and needs a restart after changing. Tuner count controls the capacity reported to clients. See Clients for setup.

docs.title: System
docs.text: The System section covers Tunarr's core infrastructure settings including backup management, logging configuration, and other server-level options.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:

    Configure automatic backups, manage backup retention, and learn how to restore your Tunarr installation from a backup.

  • Logging

    Configure log levels, log file rotation, and learn how to access logs for troubleshooting.

  • Troubleshooting

    Diagnose streaming issues for individual programs by analyzing the full transcoding pipeline.

docs.title: Quick Links
docs.text:
• Environment Variables - Server, logging, and search configuration via environment variables
  • FAQ - Frequently asked questions including the Meilisearch data.ms file

docs.title: Settings-file compatibility
docs.text: Settings files upgrade to version 2 on startup. Unused Plex streaming settings (plexStream) and XMLTV image caching (xmltv.enableImageCache) are removed while active settings are preserved. The retired /api/plex-settings endpoints are no longer available.

docs.title: Backup & Restore
docs.text: Tunarr provides a backup system that creates compressed archives of your configuration, database, and media assets. Backups can be scheduled to run automatically or triggered manually.

docs.title: What Gets Backed Up
docs.text:
A Tunarr backup archive includes:

Item Description db.db SQLite database containing channels, programs, and configuration settings.json System settings and media source configurations channel-lineups/ Channel lineup data and M3U files images/ Channel logos, artwork, and thumbnails cache/ Cached subtitles, posters, banners, fanart, and watermarks ms-snapshots/ Meilisearch index snapshots (optional) *.xml XMLTV output files

docs.title: Search authentication key in this fork
docs.text: Keep a separate, private copy of meilisearch-master-key from Tunarr's data directory alongside your backups. The built-in backup archive does not include this file. Restore it before starting Tunarr and restrict its permissions to the account running Tunarr (chmod 600 meilisearch-master-key on Unix). The file contains a credential; do not include it in support reports.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Backup settings can be configured in the Tunarr web UI under Settings > General > Backups, or via the API.

docs.title: Backup Options
docs.text: Option Default Description Enable this backup schedule true Enable or disable one configured backup schedule Schedule Daily at 4:00 AM When to run automatic backups Backup folder {data directory}/backups/ Where backup files are stored Temporary backup folder OS temporary directory Staging directory used while creating an archive Archive Format tar Archive format: tar or zip Gzip Compression false Enable gzip compression (tar only) Backups to keep 3 Number of backups to retain before deleting oldest

docs.title: Configuration controls
docs.text:
Each configured backup has an Enable this backup schedule switch. Turning it off preserves its schedule and output settings so it can be enabled again later. If settings.json contains multiple configurations, the page shows controls for each one.

Temporary backup folder selects the staging directory used while creating the archive. Leave it empty to use the server's operating-system temporary directory. It is separate from Backup folder, where completed archives are saved.

docs.title: File Naming
docs.text:
Backup files are named using a timestamp format:

tunarr-backup-YYYYMMDD_HHmmss.tar
tunarr-backup-YYYYMMDD_HHmmss.tar.gz  (with gzip)
tunarr-backup-YYYYMMDD_HHmmss.zip

Example: tunarr-backup-20250118_040000.tar.gz

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text: Backups can be scheduled in two ways:

docs.title: Interval-Based
docs.text:
Run backups at regular intervals:

  • Every N hours
  • Every N days

Example: "Every 1 day at 4:00 AM"

On the General settings page this is three fields: Backup interval (the N), Unit (hours or days) and, for a daily schedule, Time of day.

docs.title: Cron-Based
docs.text:
Use a cron expression for more complex schedules. Under Settings > General > Backups, select Cron expression as the schedule type and edit the expression. You can also set one in settings.json, and the General settings page lets you edit it.

0 4 * * *    # Daily at 4:00 AM
0 */6 * * *  # Every 6 hours
0 4 * * 0    # Weekly on Sunday at 4:00 AM

docs.title: Via Web UI
docs.text: Navigate to Settings > General > Backups and click the Backup Now button.

docs.title: Via API
docs.text:
Trigger a backup using the tasks API:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/api/tasks/BackupTask/run"

To run the backup in the background (recommended for large installations):

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/api/tasks/BackupTask/run?background=true"

docs.title: Backup Retention
docs.text: When a new backup is created and the total number of backups exceeds the maxBackups setting, the oldest backups are automatically deleted. This helps prevent disk space from filling up over time.

docs.title: Pre-Migration Snapshots
docs.text:
Tunarr migrates its database schema automatically on startup when you upgrade to a version that requires it. Before the first pending migration runs, the database is copied to a snapshot in the data directory:

db-pre-migration-<epoch>.bak

<epoch> is the snapshot time in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. Snapshots are written next to db.db — for example ~/.local/share/tunarr/db-pre-migration-1750000000000.bak — and not in the backups/ directory. They are not part of the regular backup archive described above; they exist so that a single upgrade can be undone. A fresh install has no earlier database to protect, so no snapshot is taken; likewise, starting an already up-to-date database takes none.

If the snapshot cannot be written, Tunarr stops rather than migrating, so a copy of the pre-upgrade database is always available.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
Only the 3 newest pre-migration snapshots are kept. The per-migration db-<epoch>.bak files that full-copy migrations produce are trimmed to the newest 3 as well. The two pools rotate independently: with a single shared pool, an upgrade that ran three or more full-copy migrations would push out the snapshot taken before any of them — the one worth keeping.

Snapshots contain only the database. settings.json, images, and other files are not copied.

docs.title: Rolling Back an Upgrade
docs.text:
If a new version misbehaves after upgrading:

  1. Stop Tunarr

  2. Find the newest snapshot next to db.db in your data directory (see Backup Storage Locations for platform paths):

    ls -1t /path/to/tunarr/data/db-pre-migration-*.bak | head -1

  3. Replace the database with it:

    cd /path/to/tunarr/data
mv db.db db.db.upgraded
cp db-pre-migration-1750000000000.bak db.db

  4. Start the previous version of Tunarr — the version that was running before the upgrade

Once you are satisfied with the rollback, you can delete db.db.upgraded. Keep the snapshot itself until you no longer need the escape hatch.

docs.title: Running an Older Version Against a Newer Database
docs.text:
Tunarr refuses to start if the database records migrations that the running build does not know about, which means a newer Tunarr has already migrated it:

The database at /path/to/db.db was created by a newer version of Tunarr and cannot be
used by this one. It has 1 migration(s) this version does not know about, starting with
"20260901120000_add_something". Either run the newer version of Tunarr again, or restore
the snapshot taken before that upgrade — look for a file named *-pre-migration-*.bak next
to the database and copy it over /path/to/db.db.

This normally means you rolled back to an older Tunarr (an old Docker tag or binary) while keeping a database that the newer version had already migrated. The check runs before the pending-migration check, so such a database is never migrated further — an upgrade from the future has nothing left pending, and would otherwise pass straight through.

To recover:

  • Run the newer version again. The database is intact — it was simply written by that version.
  • Or restore the pre-migration snapshot, following Rolling Back an Upgrade, then run the older version.

Do not edit the migrations table

Deleting rows from the migrations table to get past this error does not help. The schema on disk still matches the newer version, so the older Tunarr would read data it does not understand.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
Manual Process

Tunarr does not currently have a built-in restore feature. Restoration must be done manually.

docs.title: Restore Steps
docs.text:
1. Stop Tunarr - Ensure the Tunarr server is not running

  2. Locate your data directory:

    • Docker: The path you mounted to /config/tunarr
    • Windows: %APPDATA%\tunarr
    • macOS: ~/Library/Preferences/tunarr
    • Linux: ~/.local/share/tunarr

  3. Extract the backup archive:

    # For tar archives
tar -xvf tunarr-backup-YYYYMMDD_HHmmss.tar -C /path/to/restore/

# For gzipped tar archives
tar -xzvf tunarr-backup-YYYYMMDD_HHmmss.tar.gz -C /path/to/restore/

# For zip archives
unzip tunarr-backup-YYYYMMDD_HHmmss.zip -d /path/to/restore/

  4. Copy files to the data directory:

    # Required files
cp /path/to/restore/db.db /path/to/tunarr/data/
cp /path/to/restore/settings.json /path/to/tunarr/data/

# Optional directories (restore as needed)
cp -r /path/to/restore/images/ /path/to/tunarr/data/
cp -r /path/to/restore/cache/ /path/to/tunarr/data/
cp -r /path/to/restore/channel-lineups/ /path/to/tunarr/data/

  5. Start Tunarr - The search index will rebuild automatically if not restored

docs.title: Docker Restore Example
docs.text:
# Stop the container
docker stop tunarr

# Extract backup to a temporary location
tar -xzvf tunarr-backup-20250118_040000.tar.gz -C /tmp/tunarr-restore/

# Copy to your mounted volume
cp /tmp/tunarr-restore/db.db /path/to/tunarr/data/
cp /tmp/tunarr-restore/settings.json /path/to/tunarr/data/

# Start the container
docker start tunarr

docs.title: Excluding Search Snapshots
docs.text:
Meilisearch index snapshots can be large. To exclude them from backups, set the environment variable:

TUNARR_DISABLE_SEARCH_SNAPSHOT_IN_BACKUP=true

When restoring a backup without search snapshots, Tunarr will automatically rebuild the search index on startup. This may take a few minutes depending on your library size.

Windows Snapshots

There is currently an issue in Meilisearch where snapshots do not work correctly on Windows. Until this is resolved, Windows users should disable Meilisearch snapshots.

docs.title: Excluding data.ms from Proxmox Backup Server
docs.text:
The data.ms directory contains the Meilisearch search index and can be several gigabytes in size. Since Tunarr rebuilds this index automatically on startup, there is no need to include it in Proxmox Backup Server (PBS) jobs.

PBS uses .pxarexclude files (similar to .gitignore) to exclude paths from backups. To exclude data.ms, create or edit a .pxarexclude file in your Tunarr data directory:

# Create .pxarexclude in the Tunarr data directory
# Docker example — adjust to your actual mount path
echo "data.ms/" >> /path/to/tunarr/data/.pxarexclude

The file should contain:

data.ms/

PBS will skip the data.ms directory during all future backup jobs that include that path. No PBS job reconfiguration is required — the exclusion is applied automatically when PBS encounters the .pxarexclude file.

docs.title: Default Location
docs.text:
Backups are stored in the backups/ subdirectory of your Tunarr data directory:

Platform Default Path Docker /config/tunarr/backups/ Windows %APPDATA%\tunarr\backups\ macOS ~/Library/Preferences/tunarr/backups/ Linux ~/.local/share/tunarr/backups/

docs.title: Custom Location
docs.text: You can configure a custom output path in the backup settings to store backups on a different drive or network location.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Test your backups - Periodically verify that backups can be restored successfully
  2. Store backups off-site - Copy backups to cloud storage or another machine
  3. Monitor disk space - Ensure your backup location has sufficient free space
  4. Adjust retention - Increase maxBackups if you need more recovery points
  5. Schedule during off-hours - Run backups when Tunarr is less active to minimize impact

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Tunarr provides configurable logging to help you monitor server activity and troubleshoot issues. Logs can be viewed in the console, written to files, and accessed via the web UI or API.

docs.title: Log Levels
docs.text:
Tunarr supports the following log levels, from least to most verbose:

Level Description silent No logging output fatal Critical errors that cause the application to stop error Error conditions that should be investigated warn Warning conditions that may indicate problems info General operational information (default) debug Detailed information useful for debugging trace Very detailed trace information

Additionally, Tunarr has custom levels for HTTP traffic:

Level Value Description http 25 Incoming HTTP request logging http_out 15 Outgoing HTTP request logging (to Plex, Jellyfin, etc.)

docs.title: Per-Category Log Levels
docs.text:
In addition to the global log level, Tunarr supports setting independent log levels for specific subsystems. This is useful when debugging a particular area without flooding the logs with output from the entire application.

The following log categories are available:

Category Description scheduling Logs from the channel scheduling and guide generation subsystem streaming Logs from the streaming and transcode session subsystem

A category log level overrides the global level for that category only. For example, you can keep the global level at info while setting streaming to debug to get detailed stream logs without extra noise from elsewhere.

Per-category log levels are configured in Settings > General > Logging, or via the API:

curl -X PUT "http://localhost:8000/api/system/settings" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "logging": {
      "logLevel": "info",
      "categoryLogLevel": {
        "scheduling": "debug",
        "streaming": "trace"
      }
    }
  }'

Set a category's value to null or omit it to fall back to the global log level.

docs.title: Via Environment Variables
docs.text:
The simplest way to configure logging is through environment variables:

# Set log level (overrides UI setting)
TUNARR_LOG_LEVEL=debug

# Set custom log directory
LOG_DIRECTORY=/path/to/logs

docs.title: Via Web UI
docs.text:
Navigate to Settings > General > Logging to configure:

  • Log level
  • Per-category log levels
  • Log file directory
  • Log rolling settings

docs.title: Via API
docs.text:
Update logging settings through the system settings API:

curl -X PUT "http://localhost:8000/api/system/settings" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "logging": {
      "logLevel": "debug",
      "useEnvVarLevel": false,
      "logRollConfig": {
        "enabled": true,
        "maxFileSizeBytes": 10485760,
        "rolledFileLimit": 5
      }
    }
  }'

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
Log files are stored in the logs/ subdirectory of your Tunarr data directory:

Platform Default Path Docker /config/tunarr/logs/ Windows %APPDATA%\tunarr\logs\ macOS ~/Library/Preferences/tunarr/logs/ Linux ~/.local/share/tunarr/logs/

docs.title: File Format
docs.text:
• Main log file: tunarr.log
  • Format: NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON)

Each log entry contains:

{"level":30,"time":1705574400000,"msg":"Server started","hostname":"tunarr","pid":1234}

docs.title: Log Rolling
docs.text:
Log rolling prevents log files from growing indefinitely by rotating them when they reach a certain size or on a schedule.

Rolled files to keep, under Settings > General > Logging, controls the retained rotated-file count; it must be at least 1.

Log rolling is on by default. Tunarr rotates the log every day at midnight, or sooner if it grows past 50 MB, and keeps three rotated files. That is about three days of logs at normal log levels.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Option Default Description Enabled true Enable log file rotation Max File Size 50 MB Rotate when file exceeds this size. Tunarr checks the size every 10 seconds, so the file can briefly overshoot. Rolled File Limit 3 Number of rotated files to keep Schedule Every 1 day at midnight Time-based rotation

Under Settings > General > Logging, tick Roll on schedule to set the schedule: Roll interval (the N), Unit (hours or days) and, for a daily schedule, Time of day. Turning log rolling off does not keep the schedule or the size limit; turning it back on with neither set starts from the defaults, daily at midnight and 50 MB.

Size and schedule rotation can be combined. The log rotates when either one triggers, so heavy logging at debug or trace can rotate out older days early.

Upgrading

Earlier releases left log rolling off by default. On the first start after upgrading, Tunarr turns on daily rolling for any install that had it off. Installs that already had rolling enabled keep their settings. To turn it off again, disable it under Settings > General > Logging. Tunarr will not turn it back on.

docs.title: Rotated File Naming
docs.text:
When rotation occurs:

  1. tunarr.log is copied to tunarr.log.1
  2. Existing numbered files shift up (tunarr.log.1 → tunarr.log.2)
  3. Files exceeding the limit are deleted
  4. tunarr.log is truncated and continues receiving new entries

Example with rolledFileLimit: 3:

tunarr.log      (current, active)
tunarr.log.1    (previous rotation)
tunarr.log.2    (older)
tunarr.log.3    (oldest, will be deleted on next rotation)

docs.title: Configuring Log Rolling via the API
docs.text:
curl -X PUT "http://localhost:8000/api/system/settings" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "logging": {
      "logRollConfig": {
        "enabled": true,
        "maxFileSizeBytes": 10485760,
        "rolledFileLimit": 5
      }
    }
  }'

docs.title: Via Web UI
docs.text: Access logs in the Tunarr web interface under Settings > System > Logs.

docs.title: Stream Live Logs
docs.text:
Stream logs in real-time using Server-Sent Events:

# Raw NDJSON format
curl "http://localhost:8000/api/system/debug/logs/stream"

# Pretty-printed format
curl "http://localhost:8000/api/system/debug/logs/stream?pretty=true"

docs.title: Download Logs
docs.text:
Download the log file:

# Download entire log file
curl "http://localhost:8000/api/system/debug/logs?download=true" -o tunarr.log

# Download last 1000 lines
curl "http://localhost:8000/api/system/debug/logs?download=true&lineLimit=1000" -o tunarr.log

# Download pretty-printed
curl "http://localhost:8000/api/system/debug/logs?download=true&pretty=true" -o tunarr.log

docs.title: Via Command Line
docs.text:
# Follow logs in real-time (Docker)
docker logs -f tunarr

# View log file directly
tail -f /path/to/tunarr/data/logs/tunarr.log

# Pretty-print JSON logs with jq
tail -f /path/to/tunarr/data/logs/tunarr.log | jq '.'

docs.title: Recommended Log Levels
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Level Normal operation info Investigating issues debug Detailed troubleshooting trace Minimal logging warn Performance testing error or silent

docs.title: Common Log Patterns
docs.text:
Startup messages: 

Server started on port 8000
Meilisearch started on port 7700
Loading channels...

Media source sync: 

Syncing Plex library: Movies
Found 500 items in library
Sync completed in 5.2s

Streaming issues: 

FFmpeg process started for channel 1
Stream error: Connection reset by peer
FFmpeg process exited with code 1

Search indexing: 

Indexing 1000 programs...
Index update completed

docs.title: Increasing Verbosity Temporarily
docs.text:
To temporarily increase log verbosity for debugging:

  1. Set TUNARR_LOG_LEVEL=debug environment variable
  2. Restart Tunarr
  3. Reproduce the issue
  4. Check logs for detailed information
  5. Reset log level when done

For Docker:

docker run -e TUNARR_LOG_LEVEL=debug ... chrisbenincasa/tunarr

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Higher log levels (debug, trace) generate more output and may impact performance
  • Log rolling helps manage disk space but adds slight overhead during rotation
  • Streaming logs via API maintains an open connection; close when not needed
  • Consider using info level for production and debug only when troubleshooting

docs.title: Log Output Destinations
docs.text:
Tunarr outputs logs to multiple destinations:

Destination Format Description Console (stdout) Pretty-printed Colored, human-readable output Log file NDJSON Machine-parseable JSON format

Console output includes:

  • Colored log levels
  • Timestamps
  • Source file information (in development mode)
  • Formatted messages

Example console output:

[INFO] 2025-01-18T04:00:00.000Z [ChannelService] Channel 1 started streaming
[DEBUG] 2025-01-18T04:00:01.000Z [FFmpegService] FFmpeg args: -i input.ts -c copy output.ts
[ERROR] 2025-01-18T04:00:02.000Z [StreamService] Stream failed: connection timeout

docs.title: Channel bulk actions: browser evidence
docs.text:
These 1440px light-theme captures use the generic E2E fixture, with no production data. They show the same two selected channels before hiding and after reload: visibility changes, and the toolbar offers the reverse action. The browser test also verifies M3U output, persisted channel data and one batch request per action.

Before hiding After hiding and reload

Recapture with cd e2e && TUNARR_E2E_PORT_OFFSET=12000 pnpm exec playwright test tests/channelBulkStealth.spec.ts --workers=1 after the normal E2E setup. The fixture resets its local database; run it separately from other tests using the same worktree's .data directory. Images are written to that run's test-results.

docs.title: Deletion confirmation and result
docs.text:
The deletion case creates two temporary copies of a seeded channel. One named confirmation removes both through one batch request; reload retains the three original fixture channels. The browser also verifies deleted-channel 404s and their removal from M3U. Captures disable animations so the confirmation is fully visible.

Before confirming After deletion and reload

Run tests/channelBulkDelete.spec.ts with the same command above, or run both batch specs together with one worker.

docs.title: Channel bulk actions
docs.text:
POST /api/channels/bulk/stealth changes guide visibility without replacing other channel settings. Send 1–100 distinct channel UUIDs and a boolean stealth:

POST /api/channels/bulk/stealth
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "ids": ["e08f348e-3df1-44f3-833b-68e93cb98593"],
  "stealth": true
}

Malformed, duplicate, empty or oversized ID lists return HTTP 400 with { "message": "..." } before changing any channel. A valid batch returns HTTP 200 with a result for each input ID, in the same order:

{
  "results": [
    { "id": "e08f348e-3df1-44f3-833b-68e93cb98593", "success": true }
  ],
  "refresh": { "xmltv": "succeeded", "m3u": "succeeded" }
}

A missing channel has success: false, statusCode: 404 and a display-safe message. An operation failure uses status code 500 inside its item result. Already matching channels succeed without another write. The stealth changes share an immediate transaction; if it fails, the response reports no committed successes. Other fields, filler/subtitle preferences and lineup files are preserved.

After committed changes, the server requests one XMLTV publication and one M3U refresh. These run independently and each reports succeeded or failed. When nothing changes, both report not_needed. A publication failure does not undo channel changes or change successful item results into failures. Refresh the affected guide/playlist after resolving the publication problem.

For more than 100 IDs, send sequential chunks. Publication happens once per changed chunk. After a lost or invalid response, refetch channel state before deciding what to do next: the server may have committed changes even if the caller did not receive confirmation. Do not automatically replay the mutation. Keep confirmed earlier results separate from the current unknown chunk and later chunks that were never sent.

Existing single-channel endpoints remain available. Filler lists, custom shows and smart collections keep their existing individual operations.

docs.title: Channel deletion
docs.text:
POST /api/channels/bulk/delete accepts { "ids": [...] } with the same 1–100 distinct UUID validation and ordered per-item results. Deletions run sequentially. An individual failure does not prevent later IDs from being tried.

Every item also includes a cleanup result:

{
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "e08f348e-3df1-44f3-833b-68e93cb98593",
      "success": true,
      "cleanup": {
        "status": "failed",
        "message": "Unable to remove channel redirects"
      }
    }
  ],
  "refresh": { "xmltv": "succeeded", "m3u": "succeeded" }
}

Here the channel was deleted, but redirect cleanup failed. success: true means the channel-row removal committed; it does not promise that every later cleanup or publication succeeded. Cleanup uses succeeded, failed with a safe message, or not_needed when no cleanup was necessary. A pre-commit database failure reports a failed item and any separate lineup-restoration failure. SQLite and lineup files are not one atomic transaction.

After at least one committed deletion, XMLTV and M3U are each refreshed once, independently. When nothing is deleted, both report not_needed. A cleanup or publication failure is not a reason to automatically replay deletion. After a lost response, refetch and distinguish unknown from unattempted channels as described above. Existing single-channel deletion remains compatible.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thank you for your interest in contributing to Tunarr! This guide will help you get started with development.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin, ensure you have the following installed:

  • Node.js 22 or later
  • pnpm 10.28.0 or later (do not use npm or yarn; easiest to use corepack to get the right version)
  • Git
  • FFmpeg (for testing streaming features)

docs.title: 1. Fork and Clone
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository on GitHub: chrisbenincasa/tunarr
  2. Clone your fork locally:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/tunarr.git
cd tunarr

docs.title: 2. Install Dependencies
docs.text: pnpm i

docs.title: 3. Start Development Servers
docs.text:
pnpm turbo dev

This starts:

  • Backend server on http://localhost:8000
  • Frontend dev server on http://localhost:5173/web

docs.title: Repository Structure
docs.text:
Tunarr is a monorepo with four main packages:

Package Path Description @tunarr/server server/ Node.js backend (Fastify, SQLite) @tunarr/web web/ React frontend (Vite, Material-UI) @tunarr/types types/ Shared TypeScript types and Zod schemas @tunarr/shared shared/ Utility functions shared between packages

docs.title: Root-Level Commands
docs.text:
# Install all dependencies
pnpm i

# Start all dev servers
pnpm turbo dev

# Build all packages
pnpm turbo build

# Run all tests
pnpm turbo test

# Run the typechecker
pnpm turbo typecheck

# Format code with Prettier
pnpm fmt

# Lint changed files only
pnpm lint-changed

docs.title: Server Commands
docs.text:
cd server

pnpm dev              # Start server with hot reload
pnpm debug            # Start server with debugger attached
pnpm test             # Run server tests
pnpm test path/to/test.ts  # Run a single test file
pnpm generate-openapi # Regenerate OpenAPI spec
pnpm kysely           # Run Kysely CLI for database operations
pnpm tunarr           # Run CLI commands

docs.title: Web Commands
docs.text:
cd web

pnpm dev              # Start Vite dev server
pnpm bundle           # Build production bundle
pnpm generate-client  # Regenerate API client from OpenAPI spec
pnpm regen-routes     # Regenerate TanStack Router routes

docs.title: Making Changes
docs.text:
1. Create a new branch from main, or from dev for a large feature (see base branch):

    git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout -b feature/your-feature-name

  2. Make your changes

  3. Ensure code passes all checks:

    pnpm fmt
pnpm lint-changed
pnpm turbo typecheck
pnpm turbo test

  4. Commit your changes using conventional commit format

  5. Push your branch and open a Pull Request against the branch you started from

docs.title: Adding API Endpoints
docs.text:
When adding new API endpoints, follow these steps:

  1. Define your route in server/src/api/{domain}Api.ts
  2. Use Fastify with the Zod type provider for type-safe requests/responses
  3. Register the route in server/src/api/index.ts

  4. Regenerate the OpenAPI spec:

    cd server && pnpm generate-openapi

  5. Regenerate the web client:

    cd web && pnpm generate-client

docs.title: Database Changes
docs.text:
The codebase uses both Kysely (legacy) and Drizzle ORM:

  • New code should use Drizzle ORM
  • Schema definitions are in server/src/db/schema/
  • Database migrations are in server/src/migration/
  • Access the database via DBAccess, which provides both db (Kysely) and drizzle (Drizzle) instances

docs.title: Working with Dependencies
docs.text:
When adding new services or components that need dependency injection:

  1. Define your service key in server/src/types/inject.ts
  2. Register your service in the appropriate module:
    • DBModule.ts for database services
    • ServicesModule.ts for business logic services
    • StreamModule.ts for streaming services
    • FFmpegModule.ts for FFmpeg-related services
  3. Use @injectable() decorator and @inject(KEYS.ServiceName) for constructor injection

docs.title: General Guidelines
docs.text:
• TypeScript: All code must be written in TypeScript
  • No as any: Never cast types using as any
  • Formatting: Prettier handles formatting (run pnpm fmt)
  • Linting: oxlint (config in .oxlintrc.json)
  • Pre-commit hooks: Husky + lint-staged run automatically

docs.title: Import Aliases
docs.text:
• Server: Use @/ prefix (e.g., import { foo } from '@/services/foo')
  • Web: Uses configured path aliases

docs.title: Pre-Commit Hooks
docs.text: Tunarr uses Husky and lint-staged to automatically run checks before each commit. These hooks are installed automatically when you run pnpm i.

docs.title: What Runs on Commit
docs.text:
When you commit, the following checks run automatically on staged files:

  • Prettier - Formats code and auto-fixes formatting issues
  • oxlint - Lints code and reports errors

If any check fails, the commit will be blocked. Fix the reported issues and try again.

docs.title: Bypassing Hooks (Not Recommended)
docs.text:
In rare cases where you need to skip pre-commit hooks:

git commit --no-verify -m "your message"

Warning

Only bypass hooks when absolutely necessary. All checks will still run in CI, so skipping them locally just delays catching issues.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Hooks
docs.text:
If hooks aren't running after cloning:

pnpm i  # Reinstall dependencies to set up hooks

If hooks are misconfigured or you need to reinstall them:

pnpm exec husky install

docs.title: Commit Messages
docs.text: Tunarr uses Conventional Commits for commit messages. This standardized format enables automatic changelog generation and makes the git history easier to read.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
<type>(<scope>): <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]

docs.title: Types
docs.text: Type Description feat A new feature fix A bug fix docs Documentation changes only style Code style changes (formatting, semicolons, etc.) refactor Code changes that neither fix bugs nor add features perf Performance improvements test Adding or updating tests chore Maintenance tasks (deps, build config, etc.) ci CI/CD configuration changes

docs.title: Scope (Optional)
docs.text:
The scope indicates which part of the codebase is affected:

  • server - Backend changes
  • web - Frontend changes
  • types - Shared types package
  • shared - Shared utilities package
  • docs - Documentation
  • deps - Dependency updates

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Feature
git commit -m "feat(web): add dark mode toggle to settings"

# Bug fix
git commit -m "fix(server): resolve race condition in stream cleanup"

# Documentation
git commit -m "docs: update contributing guide with commit conventions"

# Refactor with scope
git commit -m "refactor(server): migrate channel queries to Drizzle"

# Chore without scope
git commit -m "chore: update dependencies"

# Breaking change (add ! after type)
git commit -m "feat(api)!: change channel endpoint response format"

docs.title: Commit Message Body
docs.text:
For complex changes, add a body to explain what and why:

git commit -m "fix(server): handle null media duration gracefully

Previously, media items with null duration would cause the scheduler
to crash. This change treats null duration as 0 and logs a warning.

Fixes #1234"

docs.title: Closing Issues on Release
docs.text:
Fixes #1234 closes the issue as soon as the PR merges, before any release ships the fix. To keep the issue open until the fix is released, put this line in the PR description instead:

Closes-on-release: #1234
  • The line must start with Closes-on-release:. List several issues on one line: Closes-on-release: #1234, #1240.
  • When a stable release ships the PR, the release workflow comments on the issue and closes it. Prereleases don't count.
  • When an issue needs several PRs, add the line only to the PR that finishes it.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Framework: Vitest
  • Test files: Use .test.ts extension
  • Test data: Use @faker-js/faker for generating test data
# Run all tests
pnpm turbo test

# Run tests in watch mode
pnpm test:watch

# Run a single test file
cd server && pnpm test path/to/file.test.ts

docs.title: Testing a Build in Docker
docs.text:
pnpm docker-test builds your working tree into the production Docker image and runs it. Use it to test a change on real hardware, such as a GPU transcoding pipeline, on your own machine or on a remote server.

It layers three compose files from docker/test/:

Layer File Committed Base compose.yaml Yes Hardware pipeline pipelines/<name>.compose.yaml Yes Your Docker host local.compose.yaml (optional) No

Settings that differ between machines live in docker/test/.env, which is also ignored by git.

docs.title: Docker Host Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker Engine 23 or later
  • A user that can run docker without sudo
  • For the vaapi and qsv pipelines: a working GPU driver, so that /dev/dri exists
  • For the nvidia pipeline: the NVIDIA Container Toolkit

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Copy the templates:

    cp docker/test/.env.example docker/test/.env
cp docker/test/local.compose.example.yaml docker/test/local.compose.yaml  # optional

  2. Edit docker/test/.env. Set TUNARR_TEST_DATA_DIR and choose a TUNARR_TEST_PIPELINE (none, vaapi, qsv, or nvidia).

  3. Add your media mounts to docker/test/local.compose.yaml, if you need any.

  4. To run on a remote server, create a Docker context that reaches it over SSH and set TUNARR_TEST_DOCKER_CONTEXT to its name:

    docker context create my-server --docker "host=ssh://user@my-server"

Warning

Every path in .env and local.compose.yaml is a path on the Docker host. With a remote context, that is the server, not your machine. Docker creates a missing host path as an empty directory instead of reporting an error.

Warning

Point TUNARR_TEST_DATA_DIR at a directory set aside for testing, or at a copy of your data. A test build may run database migrations.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
pnpm docker-test              # Build the working tree and start it
pnpm docker-test logs -f      # Follow the logs
pnpm docker-test config       # Print the merged compose file without running anything
pnpm docker-test down         # Stop and remove the container
pnpm docker-test repro        # Run the stream-repro script in a throwaway container

pnpm docker-test repro builds the same image and runs .claude/skills/stream-repro/scripts/repro.mjs inside a throwaway container with the pipeline's GPU, then copies its report back to a local temp directory. Options after repro go to the script; see .claude/skills/stream-repro/SKILL.md.

Any other arguments are passed to docker compose. The build includes uncommitted changes. The server listens on port 8001 by default, so the web UI is at http://<docker-host>:8001/web.

docs.title: Adding a Pipeline
docs.text: Add docker/test/pipelines/<name>.compose.yaml containing only the settings that pipeline needs. TUNARR_TEST_PIPELINE=<name> then selects it.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
• Fastify for HTTP server with Zod type provider
  • Inversify for dependency injection
  • Drizzle ORM (preferred) and Kysely (legacy) for database access
  • better-sqlite3 for SQLite database
  • Meilisearch for search functionality

Key directories:

  • api/ - Route handlers organized by domain
  • db/ - Database layer and schema
  • services/ - Business logic
  • stream/ - Video streaming pipeline
  • ffmpeg/ - FFmpeg wrapper and pipeline builder
  • external/ - API clients for Plex, Jellyfin, Emby

docs.title: Web
docs.text:
• React 18 with TypeScript
  • Vite for bundling
  • Material-UI v7 for components
  • TanStack Router for file-based routing
  • TanStack Query for data fetching
  • Zustand for state management
  • React Hook Form + Zod for forms

The theme lives in web/src/theme.ts: the type scale, the colours for the light and dark schemes, and the component defaults. web/src/theme.test.ts fails if a text colour falls below WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) on the page or paper background in either scheme.

The UI font is IBM Plex Sans, from @fontsource-variable/ibm-plex-sans. It is licensed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1; the licence text is in web/node_modules/@fontsource-variable/ibm-plex-sans/LICENSE after pnpm i. The font files are part of the web build, so the UI loads no fonts from the internet.

Key directories:

  • routes/ - File-based routing
  • components/ - Reusable components
  • hooks/ - Custom React hooks
  • store/ - Zustand stores
  • generated/ - Auto-generated API client

docs.title: Settings pages
docs.text:
A settings page is only its fields. It puts them inside SettingsForm (web/src/components/form/SettingsForm.tsx) and saves through useSettingsMutation (web/src/hooks/useSettingsMutation.ts). The XMLTV page (web/src/pages/settings/XmlTvSettingsPage.tsx) is the reference:

const form = useForm<XmlTvSettings>({ defaultValues: defaultXmlTvSettings, mode: 'onTouched' });
// Load the saved settings into the form; they become what it compares against.
// Skip a reload that matches them (the refetch after a save), or edits made
// while the save was in flight are lost
const { defaultValues } = form.formState;
useEffect(() => {
  if (!isEqual(data, defaultValues)) form.reset(data);
}, [data]);

const saveMutation = useSettingsMutation({
  form,
  mutation: putApiXmltvSettingsMutation(),
  toFormValues: (saved) => saved, // what the form holds once saved
  invalidate: { predicate: invalidateTaggedQueries('Settings') },
});

return (
  <SettingsForm
    form={form}
    onSubmit={(settings) => saveMutation.mutate({ body: settings })}
    isSubmitting={saveMutation.isPending}
    onRestoreDefaults={() => form.reset(defaultXmlTvSettings, { keepDefaultValues: true })}
  >
    {/* fields */}
  </SettingsForm>
);

What every settings page gets from the shell:

  • One save bar at the bottom of the form. "Restore defaults" is on the left, only when the page passes onRestoreDefaults. "Reset changes" and Save are on the right. The labels come from useActions().
  • Save is the page's only contained button. It is enabled only when the form has changes, they are valid, and no save is in flight. While a save is in flight it shows a spinner.
  • "Reset changes" appears only while there are changes, and puts the saved values back.
  • "Restore defaults" fills in the defaults without saving. Use form.reset(defaults, { keepDefaultValues: true }) so they count as a change: Save and "Reset changes" work, and leaving the page asks first. Pass undefined to hide the button, for example while the form already holds the defaults.
  • The unsaved-changes guard (UnsavedNavigationAlert) is mounted. Leaving the page, reloading or closing the tab with changes asks first. A form that spans routes passes exceptTargetPaths.
  • A save that works makes toFormValues(response, variables) what the form compares against, and every field takes those values except the ones the user changed after pressing Save. Those keep the user's value and stay unsaved, so the form stays dirty and the guard stays on. It refetches the invalidate queries and toasts "Saved". A save that fails toasts "Could not save settings: " and the server's reason, and keeps the user's changes.

Use mode: 'onTouched': Save turns off as soon as a value stops being valid, and a field shows why once the user has left it. The settings pages are General, Guide (XMLTV), Transcoding (FFmpeg), Scanner, Tuner (HDHR) and Features; the transcode-config table on the Transcoding page sits below its form, outside it.

Build the fields from the typed controllers in web/src/components/util/TypedController.tsx rather than wiring Controller by hand: NumericFormControllerText, CheckboxFormController, SwitchFormController (a switch with its label and help text) and SelectFormController (a select with its label, { value, label } options and help text; a number field stays a number).

docs.title: Entity editors
docs.text:
The channel, filler list, custom show, time slot and random slot editors sit in the same SettingsForm and save through useSettingsMutation, with failureMessage: useToasts().couldNotSave (their failures are not about settings). SettingsForm has props for what an editor needs beyond a settings page:

  • isNew: the form creates something. Save is enabled whenever the values are valid, changed or not.
  • hasOtherChanges and onDiscardChanges: changes held outside the form's fields, such as the program list in the filler list or custom show draft in the store, or a slot editor's refreshed preview. They count as changes for Save, "Reset changes" and the unsaved guard. onDiscardChanges puts them back; it runs after "Reset changes" resets the fields, and when the user leaves through the guard.
  • saveDisabled: keeps Save disabled for a reason the validation doesn't cover, such as an empty program list. The page says why.
  • disabled: locks the fields. Pass the mutation's isPending while a create is in flight, because the page moves on once it is saved and an edit made meanwhile would be lost. The filler list, custom show and slot editors lock for every save, because the draft outside the form is saved as it was when Save was pressed.

A create moves on with navigate({ ..., ignoreBlocker: true }) from the mutation's onSuccess: the save has left the form clean, but the guard still holds the state from before it until it renders again. A form that spans routes, such as an editor and its add-programs page, passes those routes in exceptTargetPaths. The guard never blocks a navigation that only changes the query string, such as the channel editor's tabs.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
• GitHub Issues: Report bugs or request features
  • Discord: Join the community for discussion and support

docs.title: Pull Request Policy
docs.text: These rules apply to every PR, however it was written. They apply to maintainers too.

docs.title: You own every line
docs.text:
• You are the author of everything in your PR, whoever or whatever typed it.
  • You must understand each change well enough to explain it in review.
  • You must have run the change yourself and confirmed it does what the PR says.
  • "The AI wrote that part" is not an answer to a review question.

docs.title: Design before code
docs.text:
Some changes need an agreed design before anyone writes code. Open an issue first and describe the design. A maintainer approves it by adding the design approved label. Then open the PR and link the issue in the "Design issue" section of the PR description.

A change needs a design issue if it does any of the following:

  • Adds a new media source type or a new kind of stream source
  • Changes the database schema (adds a migration)
  • Adds a new runtime dependency
  • Adds a new top-level feature, such as a new page, settings area, or scheduling mode
  • Changes code in more than one package (server, web, types, shared) in a way that changes how they talk to each other, such as a new API shape or shared type
  • Changes more than 500 lines outside tests, or more than 1,500 lines including tests. Neither count includes the generated files listed below.

The line counts leave out these generated files:

  • pnpm-lock.yaml
  • server/src/migration/db/sql/meta/
  • server/src/generated/, web/src/generated/, docs/generated/
  • web/src/routeTree.gen.ts
  • web/src/locales/

The design issue should cover:

  • The problem, and who has it
  • The approach, and the main alternatives you rejected
  • Which parts of the codebase change, and any schema or API changes
  • How you will split the work into PRs that can each be reviewed on their own

Large mechanical changes, such as a rename or the same fix repeated across many files, can skip the size limit. A maintainer decides by adding the mechanical label to the PR. The other triggers still apply. If you're planning a big mechanical change, ask in an issue first, because it may conflict with other open work.

Small fixes, docs changes, and refactors inside one module don't need a design issue. If you're unsure, ask in an issue or on Discord before you start.

docs.title: PRs that skip the design step
docs.text:
A bot checks every PR from an outside contributor. It detects the size limit, new migrations, new runtime dependencies, and new media sources. Maintainers flag the other triggers by hand.

When a PR needs a design and doesn't link an approved one, it gets converted to a draft and labeled needs design. The bot leaves a comment that lists what triggered it. The code stays where it is. Open a design issue and link it from the PR. When a maintainer labels the issue design approved, the bot re-checks every PR that links it and removes needs design. Rework or split the PR to match the design and mark it ready for review.

A PR labeled needs design for 30 days without an approved design will be closed. The clock pauses while the PR links an open design issue (labeled design proposal), since the PR is then waiting on a maintainer. If the design issue is closed without approval, a new 30 days starts.

Maintainers are the people listed in .github/CODEOWNERS. The bot doesn't check their PRs, but the same rules apply to them.

The bot doesn't check PRs opened before October 10, 2026. Maintainers may still apply these rules to them by hand.

The bot re-checks a PR whenever it's pushed, edited, labeled, or reopened. To re-check it without changing anything, comment /recheck on the PR. Only the PR author and people with write access can do this. Maintainers can also run the PR Policy workflow from the Actions tab with a PR number.

docs.title: Open PR limit
docs.text: Each outside contributor may have up to 5 PRs open for review at once. When you open a sixth, the bot converts it to a draft and says why. Mark it ready for review once one of your other PRs is merged or closed. Drafts don't count toward the limit, and PRs opened before the policy took effect do.

docs.title: During review
docs.text:
• Address each comment with a change scoped to that comment. Don't regenerate or rewrite unrelated code, because that forces the reviewer to start over.
  • If you don't know why your code does something, say so. Then find out before you change it.
  • A PR whose author can't answer questions about their own code will be closed.
  • A PR that doesn't follow this policy or the AI use rules is labeled needs policy fix. The bot applies it when the "AI use" section is missing or contradicted by the commits, and removes it once that's fixed. A maintainer applies it by hand for anything else and comments with what to change.
  • A PR labeled changes requested or needs policy fix with no activity for 30 days gets a warning comment. If nothing happens in the next 7 days, it is closed. Any push or comment resets the clock. Draft PRs are exempt.

docs.title: AI Use
docs.text: You may use AI tools to write code, tests, docs, and issues for Tunarr. The Pull Request Policy applies the same way with or without AI. The rules below add to it.

docs.title: Disclose AI use
docs.text:
Every PR description says whether you used AI tools, in the "AI use" section of the PR template. If you did, name the tools and say what they did. For example:

  • "Claude Code wrote most of the implementation. I wrote the tests and reviewed every change."
  • "No AI tools used."

Disclosure is not a mark against your PR. It tells the reviewer where to look harder.

  • Autocomplete that finishes the line you're typing doesn't need disclosure. Anything that writes whole functions, files, or changes does.
  • Commit trailers such as Co-Authored-By are fine to keep but don't replace the PR statement. If your commits or PR description credit an AI tool and your "AI use" section says you used none, the bot will ask you to fix the section.

A maintainer may ask how you used AI. If your answer turns out to be false, the review ends and the PR is closed. Maintainers act on concrete evidence, such as AI tool trailers in your commits or your own statements. They don't act on how the code looks. Without such evidence, they ask questions about the code instead.

docs.title: AI in review replies
docs.text: Write review replies yourself. You may use AI to understand a comment or check your answer, but don't paste model output into the thread.

docs.title: Issues and bug reports
docs.text:
AI can help you write an issue, but the content must come from you.

  • Bug reports. Report what you saw. Your steps, logs, and screenshots must come from your own Tunarr install. If you include a guess about the cause, mark it as a guess. You may include an AI analysis of the cause, but put it in the bug template's "AI analysis" field and say whether you checked it. Maintainers treat unchecked AI analysis as a lead, not a finding.
  • Feature requests. Describe the problem you have and how you would use the feature. A short request from you beats a long spec from a model.
  • Design issues. A design issue is held to the same rule as a PR. You must understand the design and be able to answer questions about it. Use the "Design proposal" issue template, which asks you to disclose AI use.
  • Comments. Don't answer other people's questions with AI output you haven't checked.

Issues that are mostly unchecked AI output will be closed.

docs.title: Security reports
docs.text:
Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub's vulnerability reporting, not in a public issue. See SECURITY.md.

A report must include steps that reproduce the problem against a real Tunarr build. Output from an AI or a scanner that you haven't confirmed will be closed without a detailed response.

docs.title: Pull Request Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Base branch
    1. Target the main branch by default. This includes fixes, chores, refactors, and small to medium features, even when they add a database migration.
    2. Target the dev branch only for large features that will need many prerelease iterations before they reach stable, such as infinite schedules or remote streaming sources. Ask in the issue or on Discord if you're unsure.
  2. Keep PRs focused - one feature or fix per PR
  3. Use conventional commits - follow the commit message format
  4. Ensure all checks pass before requesting review
  5. Update documentation if your change affects user-facing behavior
  6. Add tests for new functionality when applicable

docs.title: Settings API
docs.text:
Read a settings section with GET /api/settings/{section} and update it with PUT /api/settings/{section}. The sections are ffmpeg, xmltv, hdhr, media-source, system and feature-flags. A successful update returns the saved section; feature flags also return their metadata and environment-override status.

PUT accepts partial objects. An omitted field is preserved, including fields in nested objects such as hdhrCaptionAppearance, logging.logRollConfig and server.searchSettings. Arrays replace the whole array, rather than merging by index: send a complete language preference list or backup configuration list. Validation and server errors use { "message": "..." }.

For example, this changes only the server port and keeps search settings:

PUT /api/settings/system
Content-Type: application/json

{ "server": { "port": 8001 } }

To clear optional log-rolling schedule or maxFileSizeBytes, or search maxIndexingMemory, send null for that field. Logging category levels also use null to return to the inherited level. Omission means preserve, not clear. Disable backups with backup: { configurations: [] }.

The XMLTV outputPath remains server-owned and ignores a submitted value. System response metadata, such as dataDirectory and environmentLogLevel, is read-only. Media rescan intervals must be whole hours, at least one; saving a changed interval reschedules scans and collection/custom-show syncs without a restart.

docs.title: Subtitle preference storage
docs.text:
ffmpeg.subtitlePreferences stores an ordered list of global subtitle defaults. Each row requires languageCode, filter, allowExternal and allowImageBased. Language codes are known lowercase three-letter ISO 639-2 codes; bibliographic aliases such as ger normalize to deu. Filters are none, forced, default and any.

PUT /api/settings/ffmpeg
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "subtitlePreferences": [
    { "languageCode": "eng", "filter": "any", "allowExternal": true, "allowImageBased": false }
  ]
}

Omitting this field preserves its saved value, including through the deprecated FFmpeg settings alias. An explicit [] clears it. Old settings files load with []; malformed saved rows stop loading before defaults can replace the file. Settings file version 2 and FFmpeg config version 5 are unchanged.

Channel responses include subtitlePreferenceMode: "inherit" | "custom". Channel writes may omit the mode to preserve it on update. Creation derives an omitted mode from the supplied rows: a nonempty custom list selects custom, otherwise inherit. Switching to inherit retains custom rows. An omitted channel preference list preserves rows; an explicit [] clears them. Existing channel rows retain the legacy wire key langugeCode; global rows use languageCode.

Inheriting channels resolve the current global list for future stream selections. Each inherited row keeps its own language, filter and external/image flags; none rows are skipped and an all-none or unmatched nonempty list selects no subtitle. Custom rows retain legacy selection behavior. Empty effective lists retain each stream path's existing fallback: profile selection requires a default-marked stream, while direct selection tries default or first. Existing explicit profiles keep precedence in profile-based playback; Direct v2 gains no profile support. Direct output remains text-only.

Preferences do not enable subtitles, extraction, captions or WebVTT capabilities. An active program keeps its selected subtitles. The Captions & audio settings page edits the global list; each channel's Streaming tab selects inheritance or a custom list and previews saved globals. Fixed output audio layouts stay per channel.

docs.title: Compatibility window
docs.text:
The following GET/PUT aliases remain for the release introducing the canonical paths. They are deprecated in OpenAPI and can be removed in the following release.

Alias Canonical path /api/ffmpeg-settings /api/settings/ffmpeg /api/xmltv-settings /api/settings/xmltv /api/hdhr-settings /api/settings/hdhr /api/system/settings /api/settings/system /api/system/feature-flags /api/settings/feature-flags

/api/settings/media-source already had the canonical path. The deprecated PUT /api/system/settings/backup remains for the same compatibility window; new clients send { "backup": { ... } } to /api/settings/system.

The unused POST reset endpoints at /api/ffmpeg-settings, /api/xmltv-settings and /api/hdhr-settings are removed. This is an explicit exception to the alias window: the UI already stages defaults locally and saves them through PUT, so “Restore defaults” remains an undoable edit until Save is pressed. API clients that used POST reset must submit their desired defaults explicitly through PUT.

docs.text: A PR that is part of a parallel wave writes its note here as <date>-<slug>.md, in the same entry format as FORK.md (a ### <title> (<date>, PR #<n>) heading, then What you saw / Cause / Fix / Tests / Upstream), so parallel PRs do not conflict on FORK.md.
